title: Phonological Posterior Probabilities as Interpretable Markers of Articulatory Impairment in Motor Speech Disorders.
abstract: This study examined whether phoneme-level posterior probabilities generated by an articulatory-informed deep learning model (Phonet) can serve as interpretable and sensitive markers of articulatory impairment in motor speech disorders (MSDs). The goal was to determine whether these features distinguish individuals with and without MSDs and reflect varying severity levels of articulatory impairment.A total of 676 participants (199 with MSDs, 477 without MSDs) completed a remotely captured word repetition task. Speech recordings were phonetically aligned, and posterior probabilities were extracted using a retrained version of the Phonet model, which estimates frame-level probabilities for 23 phonological classes. Segment-level posterior values were computed and compared across groups and severity levels using linear mixed-effects regression models.Posterior probabilities were significantly reduced in the MSD group across all phoneme types. Within the MSD group, posterior probabilities decreased progressively with greater clinical severity, as measured by both perceptual sound distortion ratings and a cumulative articulation error score. Segment-specific analyses revealed systematic differences across phoneme classes, indicating that posterior probabilities capture distinct patterns of articulatory degradation associated with motor speech impairment.Phoneme-level posterior probabilities serve as interpretable, segment-specific indicators of articulatory impairment in MSDs. These features differentiate clinical status and reflect gradations of severity, making them promising tools for augmenting traditional perceptual speech assessments. Their linguistic transparency and scalability support future clinical applications in diagnosis, monitoring, and targeted intervention.

title: Expert Perspectives on Disruptive Bleeding and Hemostasis Optimization in Primary and Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Structured Expert-Opinion Survey.
abstract: Despite advances in perioperative blood management, disruptive bleeding after total hip arthroplasty (THA) remains clinically important, given associations with hematoma, wound complications, infection, reoperation, and resource utilization. The term "disruptive bleeding" has emerged from recent outcomes and health-economic work to describe bleeding-related events that alter care, but has not been standardized as a clinical entity in THA. This survey explored whether this construct aligns with arthroplasty surgeons' perspectives and identified domains for future validation.A structured expert-opinion survey was distributed to 14 arthroplasty surgeons experienced in primary and revision THA. Domains included definitions of disruptive bleeding, risk factors, intraoperative diffuse oozing, postoperative drainage, escalation triggers, and topical hemostatic agent use. Responses included categorical selections, Likert-style ratings, and free-text comments. Descriptive statistics and exact denominators were reported. An agreement of at least 70% was used descriptively to identify high-agreement items.All respondents supported characterizing disruptive bleeding as a composite of care-altering events, including symptomatic or management-changing hemoglobin decline greater than three g/dL, transfusion, prolonged drainage, return to the operating room, embolization, and readmission. The most frequently identified bleeding risk factors were thrombocytopenia and anticoagulant use (n = 14 of 14), followed by coagulopathy and liver disease (n = 12 of 14). Escalation triggers included suspected arterial bleeding (n = 14 of 14), enlarging hematoma (n = 13 of 14), hemodynamic instability (n = 13 of 14), neurovascular compromise (n = 13 of 14), and persistent drainage (n = 12 of 14). Only four of 14 supported routine topical hemostatic agent use in primary THA, whereas seven of 14 supported selective consideration in revision THA. Disagreement remained regarding timing definitions and drainage thresholds.Disruptive bleeding in THA was viewed as a composite construct defined by care-altering events rather than numeric blood-loss measures. These findings are exploratory, hypothesis-generating, and identify candidate domains for future multidisciplinary and prospective validation.Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

title: Phase 2 Trial of Icotrokinra for Patients with Ulcerative Colitis.
abstract: Monoclonal antibodies targeting the interleukin-23 pathway are effective in treating inflammatory bowel disease. However, these therapies must be administered intravenously or by subcutaneous injection.We conducted a phase 2b, double-blind, randomized trial of oral icotrokinra, a peptide that blocks the interleukin-23 receptor, in adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis. Participants were assigned to receive icotrokinra at a once-daily dose of 400 mg, 200 mg, or 100 mg or placebo. The primary end point was clinical response at week 12. Secondary end points included clinical remission, remission of symptoms, and endoscopic improvement at week 12.A total of 252 participants underwent randomization: 63 were assigned to the 400-mg group, 62 to the 200-mg group, 64 to the 100-mg group, and 63 to the placebo group. All the doses of icotrokinra were superior to placebo with respect to a clinical response at week 12, which occurred in 63% of the participants in the 400-mg group, 58% in the 200-mg group, and 55% in the 100-mg group, as compared with 27% in the placebo group (P<0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). The percentage of participants with clinical remission at week 12 was also significantly higher in the 400-mg group than in the placebo group (30% vs. 11%, P = 0.006), as were the percentage of participants with symptomatic remission (46% vs. 19%, P<0.001) and the percentage of participants with endoscopic improvement (37% vs. 14%, P = 0.002). title: Age-related disruptions in ubiquitination and mitochondrial proteostasis are associated with neuronal compartment-specific mitochondrial changes.
abstract: Declining aerodigestive neuromotor function is a major aspect of human aging, with impaired airway defense and swallow manoeuvres implicated in pneumonia and dysphagia. Hypoglossal motor neurons (MNs) innervate tongue muscles, essential for these behaviours. Their degeneration contributes to age-related aerodigestive dysfunctions. In neurodegenerative diseases, the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is altered, disturbing mitochondrial proteostasis. We have previously shown reduced mitochondrial abundance, dysfunction and mitochondrial fragmentation in aging hypoglossal MN somas and dendrites. However, the relationship between the UPS (pUBS65 and ubiquitinated proteins), mitochondrial fragmentation (pDRP1S616) and fusion promoting proteins (MFN2) in MN aging is unexplored. In other neurons, aging changes mitochondria within axons in an opposite way to somas and dendrites. We used Western blotting to show impairment in mitophagy-related pUBS65, increased fragmentation-promoting pDRP1S616 and unchanged MFN2. Serial Block-Face Scanning Electron Microscopy showed increased mitochondrial volume density and larger, more simplistic mitochondria in old, myelinated hypoglossal axons, while somas and dendrites showed reduced mitochondrial volume density and increased fragmentation. Our results suggest that a more nuanced compartment-specific evaluation of mitochondrial structure and function is required to fully elucidate the pathophysiology underlying age-related neuromotor dysfunction.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. llm_summary: Researchers examined age-related changes in hypoglossal motor neurons, which control tongue muscles critical for swallowing and airway protection, because their degeneration contributes to pneumonia and swallowing difficulties in older adults. Using Western blotting and electron microscopy, they investigated whether aging disrupts the ubiquitin-proteasome system (which normally clears damaged proteins) and mitochondrial structure in different neuronal compartments—the cell body, dendrites (input branches), and axons (output branches). The study found impaired mitophagy signaling, increased mitochondrial fragmentation markers, and compartment-specific changes: axons showed increased mitochondrial volume with larger, simpler structures, while cell bodies and dendrites showed reduced mitochondrial volume with increased fragmentation. These compartment-specific differences suggest that aging affects mitochondrial organization differently depending on neuronal location, which may contribute to age-related motor dysfunction. The authors conclude that future research must evaluate mitochondrial changes separately across different neuronal compartments to fully understand the mechanisms underlying age-related decline in motor control.

title: Trends and Projections in Valvular Heart Disease Mortality Among Older Adults in the United States, 1999 to 2040.
abstract: Valvular heart disease (VHD) contributes substantially to cardiovascular mortality. We evaluated long-term VHD mortality trends among older adults to inform healthcare planning. CDC WONDER mortality data (1999 to 2023) were analyzed for adults aged ≥65 years to calculate age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs). Joinpoint regression identified temporal trends, alongside a subtype analysis stratifying AAMRs by nonrheumatic aortic (ICD-10 I35), mitral (ICD-10 I34), tricuspid (ICD-10 I36), and chronic rheumatic (ICD-10 I05 to I09) valve disorders. Age-period-cohort modeling assessed generational effects, and ARIMA models projected mortality rates through 2040. Among 1,204,490 VHD deaths, the AAMR declined from 1999 to 2018 (annual percent change [APC] -0.87) but significantly increased from 2018 to 2023 (APC 1.52). Nonrheumatic aortic valve disorders accounted for the vast majority of deaths, demonstrating a continuous decline (APC -0.20). Tricuspid valve disorders showed a sustained rise (APC 7.30), mitral valve disorders exhibited a biphasic pattern reversing after 2012, and chronic rheumatic diseases showed a post-2017 resurgence. Mortality was highest among non-Hispanic White individuals, men, nonmetropolitan residents, and in the West. Age-period-cohort analysis demonstrated generational divergence: recent cohorts experienced lower mortality at ages 65 to 69, whereas adults aged ≥85 years faced progressively higher risks. Forecasting models project the recent resurgence will transition into a sustained plateau, stabilizing at 109.2 deaths per 100,000 population through 2040. Ultimately, after 2 decades of decline, the VHD mortality trend reversed course and is projected to remain stably elevated. This disproportionate impact among the oldest-old and rural populations underscores the need for targeted strategies to mitigate widening disparities.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. title: High-intensity interval training attenuates post-myocardial infarction remodeling and ITGAM-mediated M4 macrophage polarization.
abstract: While the pro-inflammatory M4 macrophage phenotype contributes to cardiovascular pathogenesis, its specific involvement in chronic post-myocardial infarction (MI) remodeling and responsiveness to different exercise modalities remain unexplored. We hypothesized that high-intensity interval training (HIIT) confers enhanced cardioprotection compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) by mitigating M4 macrophage polarization.A murine MI model was randomized to 4-week HIIT, MICT, or sedentary groups. Cardiac function, structural remodeling, and macrophage phenotypes were evaluated, followed by transcriptomic profiling of the myocardium. For clinical translation, plasma samples from a human coronary artery disease (CAD) cohort (with/without prior MI) were analyzed. Causality was investigated in vitro using PF4-stimulated human macrophages with targeted genetic knockdown, co-cultured with AC16 ventricular cardiomyocytes.Both exercise modalities improved functional capacity and attenuated adverse remodeling post-MI, with HIIT demonstrating enhanced efficacy over MICT. HIIT significantly attenuated MI-induced M4 macrophage polarization, evidenced by diminished expression of MMP7, S100A8, and downstream pro-inflammatory cytokines. Additionally, plasma S100A8 levels were significantly elevated in post-MI patients. Transcriptomic profiling identified integrin subunit alpha M (Itgam) as a critical upstream target; while significantly upregulated post-MI, its expression was effectively suppressed by HIIT. In vitro, targeted ITGAM knockdown effectively suppressed PF4-induced M4 polarization and mitigated macrophage-mediated cardiomyocyte apoptosis.Compared to MICT, HIIT demonstrates superior efficacy in attenuating post-MI adverse remodeling, accompanied by significant suppression of pro-inflammatory M4 macrophage polarization. In vitro validations link this protective phenotype to ITGAM downregulation. These findings inform post-MI exercise regimens and highlight potential molecular targets for developing exercise mimetics.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether high-intensity interval training (HIIT) provides greater heart protection than moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) after heart attack by reducing harmful inflammation from a specific immune cell type called M4 macrophages. In a mouse model of heart attack, both exercise types improved heart function and reduced adverse remodeling over four weeks, but HIIT demonstrated superior effects in suppressing M4 macrophage activation and associated inflammatory markers like MMP7 and S100A8. Further clinical studies are needed to confirm whether these mechanistic findings translate to improved outcomes in heart attack patients undergoing different exercise regimens.

title: Association between glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use and ischemic stroke severity.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) reduce stroke incidence, but their impact on the severity of acute ischemic stroke (AIS) when events occur remains unclear. The aim of this study is to evaluate whether pre-stroke GLP-1RA use is associated with reduced ischemic stroke severity and improved post-stroke outcomes.We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the 2016-2024 data from the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Patients were categorized based on documented use of GLP-1RAs for at least six months prior to the index stroke event. After, propensity score matching, primary outcome was measured by the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), with secondary outcomes including rates of severe stroke (NIHSS ≥10), intensive care unit admission, neurological symptoms, in-hospital complications, and 30-day mortality.A total of 209,180 first-time AIS patients were identified, of whom 4773 (2.3%) were GLP-1RA users. After PSM, 4769 patients remained in each group. GLP-1RA users had lower median NIHSS (3 vs 4, p < 0.001). GLP-1RA users also had lower rates of severe stroke (18.4% vs 25.5%, p < 0.001), dysphagia/dysarthria (43.5% vs 48.0%, p < 0.001), aphasia (25.2% vs 28.7%, p < 0.001), hemiplegia/hemiparesis (37.6% vs 43.3%, p < 0.001), intracranial hemorrhage (13.2% vs 14.7%, p = 0.031), and 30-day mortality (6.3% vs 7.6%, p = 0.016).Among adult patients who suffered a first-time AIS, pre-stroke use of GLP-1RA was associated with reduced stroke severity, lower rates of symptoms and complications, and lower mortality. These findings suggest that the benefits GLP-1RA may extend beyond preventing the occurrence of cerebrovascular events.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

title: SGLT2 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with diabetes following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: A propensity-matched cohort study.
abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) recipients are at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, and diabetes mellitus (DM) is common after transplantation. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have demonstrated cardioprotective effects in diabetic populations, but their impact in HSCT recipients is unclear. We evaluated cardiovascular outcomes associated with SGLT2i use in diabetic HSCT patients.Using the TriNetX federated research network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with DM who underwent HSCT between 2014 and 2019. Patients were stratified by SGLT2i exposure. Outcomes were assessed from 100 days post-HSCT through 5 years. Primary endpoints included all-cause mortality, hospitalization, myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure exacerbation. Propensity score matching (1:1) balanced baseline characteristics.Among 11,682 diabetic HSCT patients, 1446 (12.4%) received SGLT2i. After matching (n = 1308 per group), SGLT2i use was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality at 1 year (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.41-0.71), 3 years (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.45-0.69), and 5 years (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.40-0.60; all p < 0.001). At 5 years, SGLT2i use was also associated with reduced hospitalization (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.65-0.89; p < 0.001) and heart failure exacerbation (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.68-0.95; p = 0.009). No significant differences were observed in myocardial infarction or atrial fibrillation. Findings were consistent across transplant types.SGLT2i use was associated with reduced mortality, hospitalization, and heart failure events in diabetic HSCT recipients, with associations evident early and sustained through 5 years. Prospective studies are warranted.Published by Elsevier B.V.

title: Delays in breast cancer presentation, diagnosis, and treatment in young women.
abstract: Breast cancer (BC) in young patients is often identified at later stages, which can result in poor prognosis. It is important to investigate the factors influencing care delays and how delays affect outcomes.This study included women aged ≤40 years at diagnosis of stage 0-IV BC in the Young Women's Breast Cancer Study enrolled between 2006 and 2016. Associations between patient and tumor factors and presentation delay (first symptom to provider visit, ≥90 days), diagnostic delay (presentation to diagnosis, ≥90 days), and treatment delay (diagnosis to treatment, ≥60 days) were estimated via logistic regression. Multivariable logistic models for delays were constructed via backward selection (p ≤ .05 retained). Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models tested the association between delays and disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS). Analyses were stratified by tumor subtype and stage.Among 1071 women, there were 153 presentation, 120 diagnostic, and 228 treatment delays. In multivariable models, lower annual income was associated with higher odds of presentation delay, whereas pregnancy at diagnosis, family history of BC, and triple-negative (TN) subtype were associated with lower odds. In HER2-positive luminal B tumors, presentation delays were associated with later stage (p < .001). Odds of diagnostic delay were higher for younger patients and lower for those with TN tumors. Patients with more aggressive tumor subtypes were less likely to have treatment delays. Delays were not associated with DFS or OS.In this cohort of young patients with BC, demographic and tumor factors were associated with delays in care. llm_summary: Breast cancer in young women is often diagnosed at advanced stages, which may worsen outcomes, making it important to understand what causes delays in care. Researchers examined 1,071 women aged 40 or younger diagnosed with breast cancer between 2006 and 2016, tracking delays in three phases: from first symptom to provider visit (presentation delay), from provider visit to diagnosis (diagnostic delay), and from diagnosis to treatment (treatment delay). Lower annual income was associated with longer presentation delays, while pregnancy at diagnosis and triple-negative tumor subtype were associated with shorter delays, and younger age was associated with longer diagnostic delays. Notably, delays in presentation, diagnosis, or treatment were not associated with differences in disease-free survival or overall survival in this cohort. These findings suggest that while demographic and tumor characteristics influence the timing of care in young breast cancer patients, such delays did not measurably impact survival outcomes in this study population.

Among participants, 153 experienced presentation delays, 120 experienced diagnostic delays, and 228 experienced treatment delays. Lower annual income was associated with higher odds of presentation delay, while pregnancy at diagnosis, family history of breast cancer, and triple-negative subtype were associated with lower odds; younger age and non-triple-negative subtype were associated with higher odds of diagnostic delay. Delays in care were not associated with differences in disease-free survival or overall survival.

title: American Society of Hematology 2026 Guidelines for the Management of Myelofibrosis in Adults.
abstract: Myelofibrosis (MF) is a myeloid bone marrow malignancy with a progressive clinical course marked by disease-related symptoms, splenomegaly, cytopenias, thrombosis/hemorrhage, and a risk for blast phase transformation. Treatment recommendations are based on the burden of symptoms, prognosis of the disease, and benefits/risks of each treatment modality.ASH formed a multidisciplinary guideline panel that included specialists in myelofibrosis and hematopoietic cell transplantation, as well 2 patient representatives and was balanced to minimize potential bias from conflicts of interest. The Mayo Clinic Evidence-based Practice Center supported the guideline development process, including updating or performing systematic evidence reviews (up to January 31, 2025). The panel prioritized clinical questions and outcomes according to their importance for patients and clinicians. The panel used the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, including GRADE Evidence-to-Decision frameworks, to assess evidence and make recommendations, which were subject to public comment.The panel agreed on 10 recommendations regarding prognostic testing, indications for interferon and JAK inhibitor therapy, management of MF-associated anemia, timing of transplantation, anti-platelet therapy, and iron chelation.Key recommendations of these guidelines include suggestions for extended molecular genetic testing; use of JAK-inhibition in symptomatic, lower risk MF patients; therapeutic strategies for patients with MF-anemia and JAK-inhibitor induced anemia; and considerations regarding hematopoietic cell transplantation including timing of referral and optimization prior to the procedure. title: Use of Myocardial Perfusion Imaging to Guide Prognosis and Management in Older Adults: Is There an Age Limit?
abstract: Myocardial perfusion imaging is used to guide risk stratification and revascularization decisions. We aimed to determine whether the prognostic value of ischemia on myocardial perfusion imaging and the association with early revascularization (ER) and outcomes differ across age groups.We included 73 038 patients who underwent single photon emission computed tomography (n=45 252) or positron emission tomography (n=27 786) myocardial perfusion imaging across 20 sites from 2009 to 2024. ER was defined as revascularization within 90 days post-myocardial perfusion imaging. Propensity score-adjusted Cox models evaluated the interaction between age, ischemic burden (myocardial flow reserve for positron emission tomography), and ER for the primary outcome of all-cause death or nonfatal myocardial infarction.Median age was 66 years; 45.3% were <65, 31.5% were 65 to 74, 19.1% were 75 to 84, and 4.2% were ≥85. ER was performed in 6.1%, rising to 7.0% in those aged 75 to 84 years and decreasing to 6.5% in those aged ≥85 years. During a median follow-up of 3.7 years, 10 757 deaths/myocardial infarctions occurred. Increasing ischemia was associated with lower event rates after ER versus medical therapy across most age groups, with no significant continuous age-ischemia-ER interaction (P=0.748). In an exploratory analysis of 3031 patients aged ≥85 years, this association appeared attenuated (hazard ratio for ischemia >10%: 0.90 [0.64-1.26]), although precision was limited, likely reflecting, in part, the small number of patients undergoing ER (n=198). Among positron emission tomography patients, the myocardial flow reserve×ER association did not vary with age (3-way interaction P=0.689). In analyses excluding patients with ER, ischemia remained prognostic in all age groups, though its associated risk declined with advancing age.Ischemia remains prognostic across all ages and may help identify candidates who have improved outcomes with ER. In an exploratory analysis, this association appeared attenuated in patients aged ≥85 years, a hypothesis-generating observation. Positron emission tomography-derived myocardial flow reserve may provide complementary physiological information for treatment selection in older adults.

title: Association of Irreversible Electroporation Treatment with Overall Survival in Stage III Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: DIRECT Registry Results.
abstract: Irreversible electroporation (IRE) is used in selected patients with Stage III pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but its association with survival relative to standard-of-care (SOC) therapy remains uncertain.This multicenter observational study included 137 patients from the DIRECT registry: 99 treated within an IRE-based strategy and 38 receiving SOC without IRE. Overall survival (OS) from diagnosis was evaluated using propensity-score overlap weighting as the principal adjusted analysis. Conventional inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), propensity-score matching, 3- and 6-month landmark analyses, and a time-dependent Cox model treating IRE as a time-varying exposure were sensitivity analyses. Restricted mean survival time (RMST) at 24 months was estimated.Median time from diagnosis to enrollment was 8 months (IQR, 6-10) with IRE and 4 months (IQR, 3-6) with SOC (P < 0.0001). Unadjusted median OS was 28 months (95% CI, 23-33) and 15 months (95% CI, 12-21), respectively. Overlap weighting was associated with lower mortality with IRE (HR, 0.28; 95% bootstrap CI, 0.12-0.48). Twenty-four-month RMST was 21.22 versus 16.24 months, an absolute difference of 4.99 months (95% bootstrap CI, 1.15-8.12). The time-dependent analysis attenuated but retained the association (HR, 0.59; 95% bootstrap CI, 0.37-0.94). Other sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent.An IRE-based treatment strategy was associated with longer OS than SOC without IRE. Attenuation in the time-dependent analysis indicates that treatment timing and selection contributed to the observed difference. title: Hemagglutinin and fusion proteins precede measles virus ribonucleoproteins and marshal cell-to-cell spread in airway epithelium.
abstract: Measles virus (MeV) is the most contagious human respiratory pathogen. To understand how it spreads in the airways, we infected well-differentiated primary cultures of human airway epithelial cells (HAE). We discovered that the MeV attachment protein (hemagglutinin, H), the fusion (F) protein, and the assembly organizer protein (matrix, M) reach newly infected cells ahead of, and independently from, the replicative complex proteins. To characterize the mechanisms of MeV spread, we generated a replication-deficient adenoviral vector expressing the MeV M, F, and H proteins in a doxycycline-inducible manner. This viral vector formed infectious centers that preserved epithelial function like those from MeV infection. To further dissect this process, we generated Ad vectors expressing individual MeV proteins, termed Ad-M, Ad-F, and Ad-H. Transduction of HAE with single, double, and triple Ad vector combinations revealed that Ad-F and Ad-H are necessary and sufficient to form MeV-like infectious centers. MeV enters and spreads within airway epithelia via H protein binding to adherens junction protein, nectin-4. To disrupt spread, we introduced the point mutation HY543A, a mutation previously described to inhibit nectin-4 binding, in the Ad-H vector. Co-transduction of Ad-F and Ad-HY543A did not result in MeV-like infectious center formation. Finally, we assessed whether the MeV-related paramyxovirus Nipah (NiV) attachment and fusion proteins (G and F, respectively) support cell-to-cell spread. Co-transduction of HAE with Ad-NiV-G and Ad-NiV-F did not result in infectious center formation, suggesting that decoupling of the membrane fusion apparatus function from replication is a unique feature of the MeV envelope glycoproteins.IMPORTANCEMeasles virus is a highly contagious pathogen. We characterized a mechanism by which measles virus spreads rapidly through the cells that line the human airway in an ex vivo model. We show that the proteins of the viral membrane fusion apparatus, hemagglutinin (H) and fusion (F), move independently from and reach newly infected cells before the proteins of the replicative complex. Thus, viral protein spread is assembled and arranged in order (i.e., marshaled). Using adenovirus-based vectors, we show that co-expression of H and F proteins promotes rapid sequential spread to multiple cells and the formation of infectious centers. Further elucidation of the mechanism of measles virus amplification and cell-to-cell spread within the lung may help explain its highly contagious nature.

title: Evaluating the Role of Lower Extremity Elastic Bandage in Patients with Acute Decompensated Heart Failure.
abstract: Lower extremity compression therapy has been proposed as an adjunct to mitigate diuretic resistance during acute decompensation of heart failure (ADHF). We evaluated the effect of lower leg compression with elastic bandages on diuretic efficiency in patients with diuretic-resistant ADHF.Historical cohort study enrolling adult cardiac ICU admissions with ADHF who used elastic bandages (EB) at Mayo Clinic in Minnesota from 2007 to 2017. The diuretic efficiency before and after applying EB was the primary outcome.A total of 176 patients with heart failure who received elastic bandages were included. The in-hospital mortality rate, the median hospital length of stay, and 30-day hospital readmission were 9.7%, 11.4 days (IQR 7.1-19.0), and 11%, respectively. When EB was applied, the average daily loop diuretic dosage was decreased by a mean difference of 1.19 mg per 40 mg furosemide equivalent (95% CI: 0.22 to 2.2; p = 0.016). The average post-EB diuretic efficiency was 1,355 mL (IQR 1,119, 1,590) per 40-mg furosemide, which was significantly higher than before EB application, with a mean difference of 340 mL per 40-mg furosemide equivalent (95% CI: -554, -125; p = 0.002). A higher diuretic efficiency led to lower diuretic doses. Average daily urine output before and after EB application was not different (2,642 pre-EB vs. 2,792 post-EB mL/day; 95% CI: -455 to 154; p = 0.33).EB use enhances diuretic efficacy during ADHF. The primary outcome was diuretic efficiency, measured as urine output per 40-mg furosemide equivalent, before and after elastic bandage application. title: Nuclear grading of myxoid liposarcoma robustly predicts patient outcome: a study of 280 patients.
abstract: Myxoid liposarcoma (MLPS) exhibits variable morphology and clinical behavior. Current grading systems, which rely on the proportion of round cell areas, were developed for resections, rather than core biopsies. Additionally, criteria for round cell and "transitional" areas are subjective/poorly reproducible. It has recently been suggested that nuclear grading may be superior to traditional grading in predicting the behavior of MLPS. We compared nuclear and cellularity-based grading in a large, multinational MLPS cohort. 280 MLPS (1990-2025) were reviewed; nuclear grade was assigned using a slight modification of the Kawaguchi et al. system. Disease‑specific survival (DSS), metastasis‑free survival (MFS), and disease‑free survival (DFS) were estimated and the performance of both grading systems was compared. Tumors occurred in 152 males/128 females (median 45 years of age; range 15-91 years) and predominantly involved proximal deep soft tissues. Initial diagnoses were made with needle core (149 cases) and open biopsies (131 cases). DDIT3 rearrangement was documented in 195 tumors. Nuclear grades were 1 (71 cases), 2 (121 cases) and 3 (88 cases); grades 1 and 2 were considered "low-grade" and grade 3 "high-grade". Both systems assessed 192 (69%) and 88 (31%) tumors to be low and high-grade, respectively, although there was not perfect overlap. Clinical follow-up (280 patients; median 68 months, range: 3-355 months) showed 33 local recurrences, 96 distant metastases and 63 cancer-specific deaths. Tumors with low nuclear grade demonstrated significantly better DSS, MFS and DFS; those with low conventional grade did not. Identical results were seen with tumors diagnosed by needle biopsy (149 cases). The Harrell's C-index demonstrated nuclear grading to be superior in the prediction of DSS, MFS and DFS. We conclude that nuclear grading demonstrates superior prognostic performance over conventional grading, including in tumors diagnosed by needle biopsy. title: Hemispheric Asymmetry of Neuroimaging Biomarkers in Early Onset Alzheimer's Disease: Clinical and Cognitive Outcomes.
abstract: Individuals diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease (AD) often exhibit amyloid, tau, and atrophy predominantly in the left or right hemisphere, but group-level analyses typically ignore inter-individual variability and changing asymmetry patterns when averaging data across participants in phenotypically diverse cohorts.We examined left/right hemispheric asymmetry in amyloid positron emission tomography (PET), tau PET, and cortical atrophy in sporadic early-onset AD from 585 deeply phenotyped individuals across 2 cohorts to investigate its clinical correlates. For each imaging biomarker, we computed a global asymmetry index reflecting left/right hemisphere signal difference, and an analogous asymmetry value for PET/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) voxels. We examined clinical and cognitive correlates of this asymmetry across phenotypes cross-sectionally and longitudinally in a subset of 218 participants.Both left and right asymmetry were common for all clinical phenotypes and was correlated between imaging biomarkers. Asymmetry patterns varied spatially within phenotypes, and asymmetry in tau PET and MRI volumes was related to hemisphere-dependent cognitive deficits and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Longitudinal analyses revealed stable amyloid PET asymmetry, decreasing tau PET asymmetry, and increasing MRI volume asymmetry.Hemispheric asymmetry is common in early onset AD and correlates with clinical outcomes. Our longitudinal findings suggest a time-lagged asymmetry peak in amyloid, then tau, then atrophy. Taken together, our results position asymmetry as an important feature of AD heterogeneity, as it provides insight into disease mechanisms and trajectories. llm_summary: Researchers examined hemispheric asymmetry in brain imaging biomarkers across 585 deeply phenotyped individuals with early-onset Alzheimer's disease from two cohorts to understand how left-right differences in disease patterns relate to clinical outcomes. They measured asymmetry in amyloid and tau accumulation using positron emission tomography scans and in cortical atrophy using magnetic resonance imaging, then analyzed whether these asymmetry patterns correlated with cognitive deficits and neuropsychiatric symptoms both at baseline and over time in 218 participants. These results indicate that hemispheric asymmetry is an important feature of early-onset Alzheimer's disease heterogeneity that may provide insight into disease mechanisms and individual trajectories.

title: Neurodevelopmental Blueprint in Gliomas: Toward an Ontogenetic Multimodal Integrated Therapy.
abstract: Neuroepithelial tumors, including diffuse gliomas and embryonal neoplasms, remain among the most lethal cancers despite major advances in molecular diagnostics and some novel targeted therapies for subsets of patients. A persistent barrier to progress is the lack of a unifying framework that integrates their cellular hierarchy, spatial heterogeneity, and distinctive patterns of progression. In this review, we synthesize converging evidence that neuroepithelial tumor biology represents a pathologic re-enactment of brain ontogeny. Integrating molecular, single-cell, histoarchitectonic, and anatomic observations, we propose that neoplastic transformation, aberrant lineage commitment, and dedifferentiation mirror and invert physiological ontogenetic trajectories. This ontogenetic logic provides a coherent explanation for key hallmarks of neuroepithelial tumors, including intratumoral mosaicism, directional anatomic spread, and the emergence of therapy-resistant tumor-propagating cell states. Ontogenetic multimodal integrated therapy is an anatomy-guided strategy that aligns neurosurgery, radiotherapy, and pharmacotherapy with tumor stage and ontogenetic architecture. By shifting emphasis from radiologically visible tumor bulk to compartment-based developmental logic, this framework offers testable hypotheses and a clinically oriented paradigm for diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal monitoring in patients with neuroepithelial tumors.

title: Exploration of the genetic architecture of ANCA-associated vasculitis.
abstract: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a complex autoimmune disease with distinct clinical and serological subtypes. Previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified several susceptibility loci, particularly within the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), but the broader genetic architecture and causal variants underlying AAV remain incompletely defined.We conducted a genome-wide association study including 2068 individuals with AAV and 3258 controls of European ancestry. The discovery cohort comprised a previously published GWAS dataset supplemented with newly recruited cases. Analyses were stratified by clinical (granulomatosis with polyangiitis [GPA] and microscopic polyangiitis [MPA]) and serological (proteinase 3-ANCA [PR3] and myeloperoxidase-ANCA [MPO]) subtypes. Findings were evaluated in an independent case cohort of 465 individuals. We performed conditional and joint analyses of the HLA region, functional fine-mapping, linkage disequilibrium score regression, and integrative multi-omics analyses to prioritise candidate causal variants and assess genetic correlations.We identified eight previously unreported loci and replicated four known loci associated with AAV at genome-wide significance. Within the HLA region, HLA-DPB1∗04 showed the strongest association with AAV, GPA, and PR3 subtypes, whereas HLA-DRB1∗04 was most strongly associated with MPO and MPA. Conditional analyses identified additional independent effects, including amino acid variation in HLA-DQA1. SNP-based heritability estimates indicated a substantial genetic contribution to AAV (h2 = 0·40). Genetic correlation analyses revealed shared heritability with multiple traits, including celiac disease and hypothyroidism. Integrative analyses highlighted candidate genes, including HCG9 and PRTN3, and implicated protein interaction networks involving genes related to neutrophil biology. Protein-protein interaction analysis identified networks involving genes implicated in AAV risk, including PRTN3, AZU1, ELANE, and SERPINA1.These findings expand the genetic landscape of AAV and support a complex and heterogeneous genetic architecture involving both MHC and non-MHC loci. The integration of genetic association, functional annotation, and network analyses suggests that disease susceptibility is mediated through multiple biological pathways, including immune regulation and neutrophil function. title: Benchmarking four commercial antimicrobial susceptibility testing systems and disk diffusion to reference broth microdilution in the assessment of gram-negative bacterial isolates.
abstract: Commercial antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) systems for gram-negative bacteria provide operational advantages over reference broth microdilution (BMD) testing, but the results produced by commercial AST systems might not be as accurate as the reference method. Assessing and comparing the performance of AST systems can be informative for clinical microbiology practice. In total, 280 clinical isolates and 100 isolates from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Antimicrobial Resistance Isolate Bank, including Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, were intended to be tested using disk diffusion (DD) and automated commercial AST systems, such as Selux AST System (Selux Diagnostics), MicroScan (Beckman Coulter), Phoenix (Becton, Dickinson and Company), and Vitek 2 (bioMérieux). These results were compared to BMD as the reference standard. In total, 372 isolates were assessed. For Enterobacterales, the greatest frequency of very major errors was identified with cefepime by Vitek 2 (29.0%) and ertapenem by DD (9.1%); essential agreement less than 90% was identified with the following combinations: aztreonam by MicroScan (86.4%), aztreonam by Vitek 2 (88.9%), cefepime by Selux (86.3%), cefepime by Vitek 2 (76.8%), ceftazidime by Vitek 2 (89.9%), and levofloxacin by MicroScan (83.4%). For P. aeruginosa, essential agreement less than 90% was identified with the following combinations: gentamicin by Selux (87.2%), tobramycin by Selux (86.6%), and ciprofloxacin by Phoenix (88.4%). Overall, antimicrobials that had low demonstrable bias across all automated commercial AST systems included ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, ceftazidime-avibactam, ertapenem, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Comparing commercial testing systems head-to-head against a reference standard provides insight into the strengths and weaknesses of the performance of these test systems, and these insights can subsequently inform local decisions regarding further investigations and potential operational mitigation strategies.IMPORTANCEThis study assessed and compared the performance of multiple commercial antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) systems and disk diffusion methods. The accuracy of determining minimum inhibitory concentrations or zone diameters of antimicrobials and the associated interpretive categories were studied for 372 isolates of Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Performance of the evaluated systems revealed that multiple antimicrobial-organism combinations were below the standards typically required by regulatory agencies and clinical laboratories. These deficiencies varied across the commercial platforms and disk diffusion methods, highlighting the importance of benchmarking studies that compare the performance using identical isolates. These identified performance weaknesses may warrant further study and/or the implementation of mitigation strategies in clinical laboratory operations to prevent the reporting of errant results.

title: Spinal Cord and Nerve Root Involvement in Histiocytic Neoplasms: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Study.
abstract: Histiocytic neoplasms, including Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD), Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), and Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease (RDD), have frequent nervous system involvement. The aim of this study was to characterize the neurologic, radiologic, and laboratory features of spinal cord and nerve root involvement in histiocytic neoplasms.We evaluated patients with biopsy-proven ECD, LCH, or RDD seen at a tertiary referral center between January 1996 and December 2024. Patients were included if spinal MRI demonstrated spinal cord or nerve root involvement. Spinal MRI was performed for evaluation of myelopathic or radicular symptoms or as part of staging in patients with CNS involvement. We collected demographic variables, neurologic syndromes and imaging patterns, treatment characteristics, and outcomes including disability (Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] score) and ambulatory status. The primary outcome was neurologic disability at nadir and last follow-up; secondary outcomes included radiographic patterns and clinical response to treatment. Data were summarized descriptively, with exploratory group comparisons performed using parametric or nonparametric tests as appropriate.Among 415 patients with ECD (n = 183), LCH (n = 144), or RDD (n = 88), spinal cord or nerve root involvement was identified in 42 (ECD, 27; LCH, 4; RDD, 11). The median age at onset was 43.1 years (interquartile range 32.1-58.5), and 18 (43%) were female. Most cases were symptomatic (36/42, 86%), with myelopathy as the first neurologic manifestation in 26 (72%). Parenchymal infiltration predominated in the ECD group (17/27, 63%), compared with LCH (2/4, 50%) and RDD (2/11, 18%) groups (Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.035). Root involvement was more frequent in the RDD group (8/11, 73%) than in the ECD (7/27, 26%) or LCH (1/4, 25%) group (Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.021). The median EDSS score at nadir was 4.0; 43% required ambulatory aid or worse. After treatment, 22 of 36 symptomatic patients (61%) improved clinically and radiographically, more often in RDD (10/11, 91%) and LCH (2/3, 67%) groups than in the ECD group (10/22, 46%; Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.022). At a median 5.8-year follow-up, 8 of 38 survivors (21%) required ambulatory assistance or were nonambulatory.Spinal cord and nerve root involvement occurs in histiocytic neoplasms. These findings support prioritizing spinal MRI in patients with neurologic symptoms or high-risk disease features because early identification may inform diagnosis and management.

title: Network reorganization of anterograde thalamic connectivity during non-periodic patterned deep brain stimulation.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) can reduce seizures in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. However, seizure freedom is rare, and there is no early response biomarker to predict long-term seizure suppression. To evaluate a candidate short-term biomarker of therapeutic response to DBS, we studied 18-min trials of ANT stimulation in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy undergoing intracranial electroencephalography. We compared a standard high-frequency periodic versus a non-periodic pulse pattern. We found that short-term ANT stimulation within the clinically used amplitude range preferentially altered the first 150 ms of anterograde ANT to anterior cingulate and superior frontal connectivity. Non-periodic ANT stimulation selectively modified early cortico-cortical evoked potentials more than periodic stimulation, and these changes were driven by the response phase. These pattern-specific changes in connectivity between the ANT and spatially restricted cortical areas suggest differing mechanisms and are a promising candidate biomarker for patients being treated with ANT-DBS.© 2026 The Author(s).

llm_summary: Deep brain stimulation of the anterior thalamus can reduce seizures in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, but most patients do not achieve complete seizure freedom, highlighting the need for biomarkers to predict which patients will respond well to treatment. Researchers compared how 18-minute trials of two different stimulation patterns—standard high-frequency periodic pulses versus non-periodic pulses—affected brain connectivity in 18 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy who had electrodes implanted in their brains for monitoring. Non-periodic stimulation produced greater changes in early brain signals between the anterior thalamus and specific cortical areas (anterior cingulate and superior frontal regions) compared to periodic stimulation, with these differences driven by the response phase of the stimulation. These pattern-specific changes in connectivity suggest that periodic and non-periodic stimulation may work through different mechanisms in the brain. The findings propose that early changes in thalamic-cortical connectivity could serve as a candidate biomarker for predicting long-term seizure suppression in patients receiving anterior thalamus deep brain stimulation, though further validation would be needed to confirm this potential clinical application.

title: Neurofibrillary tangle deposition in primary idiotypic isocortices using flortaucipir PET in histopathologically confirmed Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Tau deposition in Alzheimer's disease (AD) spreads throughout the brain in a stereotypical pattern captured by the Braak neurofibrillary tangle staging scheme. While involvement of primary isocortex defines the highest stage, it is unclear whether flortaucipir PET uptake differs among primary isocortical regions. We determined relationships between flortaucipir uptake in primary visual, auditory, motor, and somatosensory isocortices and Braak stage in 155 autopsy-confirmed participants with AD. Flortaucipir uptake was observed starting at Braak stage V, with visual and auditory isocortices showing greater and faster increases in uptake than somatosensory and motor; age and APOE ε4 influenced uptake. Flortaucipir uptake and change in primary isocortices were similar in the lateral temporal cortex but different in the entorhinal cortex. Findings suggest that tau deposition in primary isocortices in AD occurs earlier than currently emphasized, although there are differences among them. Given these findings, clinical correlations of primary isocortical involvement in AD need to be evaluated.© 2026 Published by Elsevier Inc.

llm_summary: Researchers examined whether tau protein deposition in primary sensory and motor brain regions follows the established Braak staging scheme for Alzheimer's disease by measuring flortaucipir PET uptake in 155 autopsy-confirmed participants. Flortaucipir uptake in primary isocortices (visual, auditory, motor, and somatosensory regions) was observed starting at Braak stage V, with visual and auditory cortices showing greater and faster increases in uptake compared to somatosensory and motor cortices. Age and APOE ε4 status influenced the level of flortaucipir uptake observed in these regions. The findings suggest that tau deposition in primary isocortices occurs earlier than currently emphasized in clinical practice, though the pattern of involvement differs among these regions. Clinical correlations between primary isocortical tau involvement and Alzheimer's disease symptoms require further evaluation to determine the relevance of these regional differences.

These findings suggest tau deposition in primary isocortices occurs earlier than currently emphasized, though regional heterogeneity exists, warranting clinical correlation studies.

title: Determinants of quality of life in patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced secondary adrenal insufficiency.
abstract: Limited data are available on quality of life (QoL) and adrenal crises in patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced secondary adrenal insufficiency (ICI-SAI).To (1) characterize the presentation, management, and outcomes of patients with ICI-SAI; (2) compare outcomes of ICI-SAI with other etiologies of secondary adrenal insufficiency (oSAI); and (3) identify variables associated with QoL and adrenal crisis.In this single-center cross-sectional study, adults with ICI-SAI or oSAI (2018-2025) completed questionnaires assessing symptoms, management, adrenal crises, and the Addison's Disease-Specific QoL survey (AddiQoL); outcomes included AddiQoL score and adrenal crisis events.Patients with ICI-SAI (n = 109) were older (median age 66 vs 60 years), more often women (59% vs 43%), and more frequently diagnosed within 1 year of symptom onset (88% vs 42%, P < .001), compared to patients with oSAI (n = 139). Patients with ICI-SAI had higher AddiQoL scores (median 87 vs 85, P = .020). In a multivariable analysis of age, sex, glucocorticoid dose and type, insurance support, and duration of SAI, ICI-SAI remained independently associated with higher AddiQoL (estimate 5.4, P = .010). The prevalence of reported adrenal crises within the prior year was similar between groups (15% vs 14%, P = .782). In a multivariable analysis, higher AddiQoL scores were independently associated with lower odds of adrenal crisis (OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.42-0.76).Patients with ICI-SAI report better QoL compared with patients with other causes of SAI, despite similar adrenal crisis rates. These differences may be related to earlier diagnosis and differing clinical contexts, underscoring the importance of timeline recognition and patient-centered management.© The Author(s) 2026. title: FGFR kinase isoform and activation state modulate ATPase activity.
abstract: Fibroblast growth factor (FGF) binding to FGF receptor (FGFR) induces trans-autophosphorylation of activation loop tyrosine residues within the receptor's intracellular kinase domain, thereby activating the receptor and promoting downstream substrate phosphorylation. Here, using activity assays and 31P NMR spectroscopy on the FGFR kinase domain, we show that phosphorylation of activation loop tyrosine residues not only enhances kinase activity but also increases the rate of ATP hydrolysis by 33-fold. This ATPase activity varies among FGFR kinase isoforms, with a 5.4-fold difference between FGFR2 and FGFR3 kinases. Conversion of ATP to ADP in phosphorylation assays also promotes the reverse phosphorylation reaction, which involves phosphoryl group transfer from phosphotyrosine to ADP to regenerate ATP. Based on these observations, we hypothesize that ATPase activity occurs in cells and may decrease the local ATP/ADP ratio surrounding FGFR. Such a mechanism would reduce the favorability of phosphorylation and may promote signal termination through reverse phosphorylation.© 2026 The Author(s).

llm_summary: Fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) are activated when phosphate groups are added to specific tyrosine residues in their kinase domains, a process that initiates cellular signaling. Researchers used activity assays and 31P NMR spectroscopy to measure how phosphorylation of these activation loop tyrosines affects both kinase activity and ATP hydrolysis rates in FGFR kinase domains. Phosphorylation increased the rate of ATP hydrolysis by 33-fold and this ATPase activity varied substantially among FGFR isoforms, with FGFR2 and FGFR3 kinases differing by 5.4-fold. The conversion of ATP to ADP during phosphorylation reactions also promoted reverse phosphorylation, in which phosphate groups transfer from phosphotyrosine back to ADP to regenerate ATP. The authors propose that this ATPase activity may occur in cells and could reduce local ATP availability around FGFR, potentially weakening phosphorylation and promoting signal termination through reverse phosphorylation.

title: Multicenter Phase I Study of Triapine in Combination with [177Lu]Lutetium-Dotatate in Patients with Well-Differentiated Neuroendocrine Tumors (ETCTN 10388).
abstract: The next generation of theranostics studies is looking at novel combinations with radiation sensitizers to enhance peptide receptor radionuclide therapy's efficacy. In this study, we present safety and efficacy data from a multicenter phase I study of a [177Lu]lutetium-dotatate-triapine combination in patients with gastroenteropancreatic (GEP) neuroendocrine tumors (NET).The study consisted of 2 phases (part A: dose escalation; part B: dose expansion) administering the recommended phase II doses (RP2D) for the 2 agents. All patients received 200 mCi of [177Lu]lutetium-dotatate on day 1 of four 8-week cycles, in combination with oral triapine administered at assigned dose levels (100, 150, or 200 mg) from day 1 to day 14 of each cycle.A total of 31 (A: 15; B: 16) patients received treatment. Across the study, 9 patients experienced dose-limiting toxicities: grade 3 anemia (n = 1), grade 5 cardiac arrest (unrelated to investigational product; n = 1), and grade 4 neutropenia (n = 7). Based on the overall safety and pharmacokinetics data, a [177Lu]lutetium-dotatate (200 mCi) plus triapine (150 mg) dose was selected as the RP2D for the expansion phase. Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events were observed in 77% of patients: anemia (23%), nausea and vomiting (3%), lymphopenia (58%), neutropenia (35%), and decreased white blood cell count (39%). The majority of cytopenias were transient and resolved within 2 weeks. Among the 28 evaluable patients, the objective response rate was 21.4%, and the median progression-free survival has not been reached (median follow-up period, 23.7 months).The combination of [177Lu]lutetium-dotatate (200 mCi) and oral triapine (150 mg D1-14) was well tolerated and demonstrated preliminary activity in patients with well-differentiated GEP-NET (NCT04234568).©2026 The Authors; Published by the American Association for Cancer Research.

title: Clinical Presentation, Misdiagnosis, and Imaging Findings of Anterior Disc Herniations.
abstract: Anterior and anterolateral lumbar disc herniations are uncommon and usually do not present with classic radicular symptoms. This contributes to a broader and sometimes misleading differential diagnosis based on the initial presentation. When identified on cross-sectional imaging performed for nonspinal indications, displaced disc material can be mistaken for a retroperitoneal mass, potentially prompting additional imaging or invasive evaluation. We report 6 cases of anterior and anterolateral disc herniations identified on CT and MRI, including some patients presenting with abdominal or flank pain. Imaging demonstrated anterior disc extrusion, some with marked inflammatory changes. In some cases, the initial diagnosis included retroperitoneal neoplasm or an inflammatory process. Recognizing this imaging pattern and its clinical context may help accurate diagnosis, avoid unnecessary procedures, and guide appropriate management.© 2026 by American Journal of Neuroradiology.

Researchers examined 6 cases of anterior and anterolateral disc herniations identified on CT and MRI imaging, some of which presented with abdominal or flank pain rather than typical spinal symptoms. The imaging findings showed anterior disc extrusion with marked inflammatory changes in some cases, and the displaced disc material was initially mistaken for retroperitoneal masses or inflammatory processes in several patients. Recognizing the characteristic imaging pattern of anterior disc herniations and correlating it with clinical presentation may help clinicians avoid unnecessary additional imaging studies or invasive procedures. This case series highlights the importance of accurate diagnosis to guide appropriate management and prevent unnecessary diagnostic workup in patients with anterior disc herniations.

title: The Congenital Heart Surgeons' Society Center for Research and Quality 2025 Annual Report.
abstract: The Congenital Heart Surgeons' Society (CHSS) is viewed by many as one of the most prestigious professional societies dedicated to pediatric and congenital cardiac surgery. The CHSS Center for Research and Quality (CRQ) Fall 2025 Work Weekend was held in Chicago on Saturday, October 25, 2025. The purpose of this article is to summarize the proceedings of the CHSS CRQ Fall 2025 Work Weekend and to provide a 2025 Annual Report of the CHSS CRQ. At the CHSS CRQ Fall 2025 Work Weekend, multiple topics were discussed related to ongoing CHSS research and quality initiatives. The CHSS CRQ is evolving to keep pace with the rapid evolution of medical informatics and the ever-evolving regulatory issues of clinical research. This 2025 Annual Report of the CHSS CRQ summarizes some of the ongoing initiatives at CHSS CRQ designed to assure that the CHSS CRQ continues to lead innovative and collaborative clinical research to improve pediatric and congenital cardiac care.

title: Sex-Based Differences in Chronic Heart Failure: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: Sex-based disparities in patient enrollment and treatment effects in heart failure (HF) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been reported. We aim to systematically analyze sex-based enrollment and treatment effect differences in HF RCTs over time.RCTs enrolling patients with chronic HF were systematically searched on PubMed-MEDLINE. Eligible trials included pharmacological or device-based interventions with a hard primary endpoint (mortality and hospitalization) and reporting enrollment of women. Sex-specific treatment effects (HR or RR) were extracted. Meta-analyses were performed using random-effects models, and pre-specified subgroup analyses were performed.A total of 56 RCTs (39 drug, 17 device) were included. The pooled proportion of women enrollment was 27.0% (95%CI: 22.0% to 32.4%) in drug trials and 25.3% (95%CI: 21.0% to 29.9%) in device trials. Women were more underrepresented in HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) than in HF with preserved EF (HFpEF) trials (21.0% vs 49.6%, p < 0.001). Among drug trials reporting sex-specific effects, the pooled sex interaction for RCTs reporting HR was 0.94 (95%CI 0.89-1.01) and RR was 0.81 (95%CI 0.68-0.96), suggesting potentially greater benefit for women. No interaction was observed between HFrEF and HFpEF trials (HR: p = 0.44; RR: p = 0.95). The pooled interaction estimate on event counts was 0.90 (95%CI 0.84-0.96). For devices, the pooled sex interaction for RCTs reporting HR was 1.05 (95%CI 0.90-1.22) and RR was 0.68 (95%CI 0.50-0.93).Women remain underrepresented in HF RCTs. Sex-stratified analyses suggest a potentially greater relative benefit of drug intervention in women, which might inform future RCTs. llm_summary: Researchers examined sex-based differences in enrollment and treatment effectiveness across 56 randomized controlled trials of heart failure interventions, finding that women comprised only 27.0% of drug trials and 25.3% of device trials, with particularly low representation in trials of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (21.0% versus 49.6% in preserved ejection fraction trials). Among drug trials reporting sex-specific outcomes, women showed potentially greater relative benefit compared to men, with pooled interaction estimates of 0.94 for hazard ratios and 0.81 for risk ratios, though device trials showed no clear sex-based difference in treatment effect. The sex-stratified analyses suggest that women may derive greater relative benefit from pharmacological interventions for heart failure, which could inform the design of future clinical trials. These findings indicate that despite women's underrepresentation in heart failure research, sex-specific treatment responses may exist and warrant further investigation. Additional research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms underlying these observed sex-based differences in treatment effectiveness.

title: A Bibliometric Analysis of Research Interest in Dupilumab for Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyposis.
abstract: The objective was to evaluate the rapid progress and interest regarding the role of dupilumab in the treatment of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis (CRSwNP).The Web of Science Core Collection database was queried in a single day for publications using terms "dupilumab" and a combination of "chronic sinusitis," "rhinosinusitis," and "polyposis" without time restrictions. Document type, years, authors, countries with economic estimates, institutions, journal information, and keywords were analyzed and visualized using VOSviewer. Only original investigation and review articles were included for analysis. Further analysis of the top 10 cited articles were performed.Following deduplication, 358 unique publications were abstracted. Most studies were published in the United States (25.7%), followed by Italy (17.9%) and Japan (9.4%). Studies were most frequently published in the International Forum of Allergy & Rhinology (n = 21) followed by The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice (n = 17). B Claus was the most cited author pertaining to this topic, and the most frequent keywords and concepts spanned outcomes, immunology, allergy, and adverse events.Research regarding the use of dupilumab in the treatment of CRSwNP is rapidly evolving, highlighting the paradigm shift in treatment with the introduction of biologic therapy. This analysis showcased global interest in this topic, highlighting hallmark publications and prolific investigators, while also identifying areas for further exploration and collaboration.

title: Classification and Outcomes of Coronary Microvascular Disease in Myocardial Infarction and Angina With Nonobstructive Coronary Arteries.
abstract: Myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCAs) and angina with nonobstructive coronary arteries (ANOCAs) present diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. We assessed the frequency of coronary microvascular disease (CMD) and its subtypes in MINOCA compared with ANOCA and evaluated long-term cardiovascular outcomes.Patients with nonobstructive coronary arteries undergoing invasive coronary function testing from 2012 to 2022 were prospectively enrolled and retrospectively classified as MINOCA or ANOCA (reference group). Myocardial infarction due to atherothrombosis, myocarditis, and Takotsubo syndrome were excluded. Invasive provocation testing was performed. CMD was classified as endothelium-independent (coronary flow reserve <2.5 with adenosine) and endothelium-dependent (<50% increase in coronary blood flow with acetylcholine). Major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiac death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, heart failure hospitalization, urgent revascularization, stroke) were recorded over 8 years.Of 622 patients, 73 (12%) had MINOCA (69% female, median age 56 years) and 549 (88%) ANOCA (72% female, median age 53 years). CMD was common in both groups (71% versus 64%; P=0.271), while endothelium-independent CMD was more frequent in MINOCA (41% versus 21%; P<0.001). Over a median follow-up of 4.5 years, major adverse cardiovascular events occurred more often in MINOCA (40% versus 11%; adjusted hazard ratio, 2.4; P=0.001). CMD predicted higher major adverse cardiovascular events in both MINOCA (hazard ratio, 3.6 [95% CI, 1.1-12.0]; P=0.038) and ANOCA (hazard ratio, 7.9 [95% CI, 2.9-21.8]; P<0.001).CMD is common in both MINOCA and ANOCA. The higher prevalence of endothelium-independent CMD in MINOCA suggests a potential mechanistic role in infarction. Patients with MINOCA have a worse prognosis than ANOCA, particularly when CMD is present.

title: An Infusion Scheduling Decision Support Tool to Manage Resource Utilization.
abstract: As demand for infusion therapy increases due to an aging population and growing rates of chronic illness, effective resource management in scheduling becomes more critical to serve patients in ambulatory infusion centers. The wide range of treatment types, lengths, and nursing requirements, as well as capacity constraints, makes infusion scheduling challenging to effectively manage patient flow and resource utilization. Despite efforts to improve scheduling efficiency, the lack of practice implication and feasibility remains. This study aims to develop a tool that delivers data- and algorithm-driven recommendations for appointment scheduling decisions to improve resource management.We introduce a real-time decision support tool that simultaneously accounts for (1) existing nursing workload and space utilization and (2) the nursing time and infusion chairs required for upcoming patients. The tool interface is presented, and the functions of each element are described. The appointment time selection algorithm was developed to provide schedulers with options for scheduling, constrained by nursing and chair availability. The tool also provides schedulers with the flexibility to deviate from recommendations and receive dynamic feedback on patient volume and nursing needs based on their decisions.The implementation results show a significant reduction in distributing nurses' workload in terms of time mismatching between patients' needs and nursing availability by 45.5%, P < .001, while the chair utilization remained consistent. The feedback from both the scheduling team and nurses was positive, which provided strong evidence for how this tool addressed and targeted their scheduling needs. In addition, key practice behaviors and implementation challenges that impact operations efficiency are discussed for further improvement.The proposed tool offers a streamlined, interactive, and adaptable scheduling approach for better resource utilization and ultimately reduces the time schedulers spend on making manual decisions.Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. title: Burden of hospitalizations in four adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer survivor populations in the United States, 2006-2020.
abstract: We describe hospitalization rates in adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer survivors 2-5 years (Y2-Y5) from diagnosis.Observational study of AYA cancer survivors diagnosed 2006-2020 was conducted in two healthcare systems [Kaiser Permanente Southern California (n=7889) and Northern California (n=7338)] and two states [California (47,302) and Utah (n=7935)]. Hospitalizations were ascertained from electronic health records and statewide administrative records and stratified by whether pregnancy-related. Hospitalization rates were calculated by cohort. We estimated patient factors associated with hospitalizations using a Poisson model.Most AYA survivors were women (~64% of all cohorts), mean age ~31 years at diagnosis, and non-Hispanic white (range 35.1-81.2%) or Hispanic (range 14.3-40.6%). Overall, 21-24% of AYA survivors experienced >1 hospitalization. Unadjusted hospitalization rates declined from Y2 [range 155.1-243.4 per 1000 person-years (PY)] to Y5 (range 105.8-132.0 PY) (p-trend<0.0001 in all cohorts). Factors associated with increased non-pregnancy related hospitalizations were [range of relative risks (RR)]: non-Hispanic Black race/ethnicity (RR 1.46-1.66 vs non-Hispanic white); public insurance (RR 1.57-1.93 vs commercial/military); receipt of chemotherapy (RR 1.51-1.81), and cancer type-breast (RR 1.69-1.97), cervical (RR 2.30-3.31), colorectal (2.76-3.66), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (RR 2.89-5.19), acute myeloid leukemia (2.11-5.05), and sarcoma (RR 2.70-4.96) (vs thyroid).While hospitalizations decline as time from diagnosis elapses across health system settings and states, nearly 1 in 5 AYA cancer survivors experience hospitalization in early survivorship.Hospitalization rates remain elevated in some AYA patient subgroups in early survivorship, highlighting the need to identify AYAs at risk to mitigate unanticipated hospitalizations and costs.

llm_summary: Researchers examined hospitalization rates among adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer survivors to understand the burden of healthcare utilization in early survivorship, studying 70,464 survivors diagnosed between 2006-2020 across two healthcare systems and two states. Overall, 21-24% of AYA survivors experienced at least one hospitalization 2-5 years after diagnosis, with hospitalization rates declining from 155-243 per 1,000 person-years in year 2 to 106-132 per 1,000 person-years in year 5 across all cohorts. Non-Hispanic Black survivors, those with public insurance, and survivors of certain cancer types including acute lymphoblastic leukemia (relative risk 2.89-5.19), colorectal cancer (relative risk 2.76-3.66), and sarcoma (relative risk 2.70-4.96) showed substantially elevated hospitalization rates compared to their respective reference groups. These findings suggest that while hospitalizations decrease over time in early survivorship, particular subgroups of AYA cancer survivors remain at elevated risk for unplanned hospitalizations.

title: Demographic Conscious Analysis: A New Paradigm for Health Research.
abstract: Race and ethnicity are frequently misused in research as biological determinants, reinforcing essentialist assumptions and embedding structural factors into clinical guidelines and tools. Disparities in health outcomes increasingly reflect lived experiences and structural inequities, yet standard analytic approaches have not meaningfully evolved. We introduce demographic conscious analysis (DCA), a methodological framework replacing the use of social demographics as predictor variables. Race/ethnicity is a "social demographic" variable that acts as a proxy for causative variables. The social demographic is excluded from primary analytic models, which instead incorporate causative variables; for race/ethnicity, these might include socioeconomic status, geographic deprivation, chronic stress, and accelerated biological aging. The social demographic is added in a secondary diagnostic analysis to assess residual confounding. A residual association signals unmeasured or inadequately captured causal mechanisms. Within a study, DCA provides a practical method to evaluate a model. Across studies, DCA offers a way to assess progress toward comprehensive measurement of the causative factors for which a given social demographic variable serves as a proxy. Overall, DCA replaces unchangeable social demographic variables with potentially modifiable causative variables. (Am J Public Health. Published online ahead of print October 15, 2026:e1-e10. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2026.308767).

llm_summary: Race and ethnicity have been misused in health research as biological determinants, which reinforces incorrect assumptions and embeds structural inequities into clinical tools and guidelines. Researchers introduced demographic conscious analysis (DCA), a methodological framework that removes social demographic variables like race and ethnicity from primary statistical models and replaces them with measurable causative factors such as socioeconomic status, geographic deprivation, chronic stress, and biological aging. In this approach, the social demographic variable is then added back in a secondary diagnostic analysis to identify any remaining associations that might signal unmeasured or inadequately captured causal mechanisms. DCA provides a practical method to evaluate whether a statistical model has comprehensively measured the actual causes underlying health disparities rather than relying on demographic proxies. This framework offers researchers a way to assess progress toward identifying and measuring the true modifiable factors responsible for health disparities across different populations.

title: Somatic epimutations cap genetic determinism in the human diploid chromatin epigenome.
abstract: Diploid human cells contain two non-identical genomes, and differences in their regulation underlie human development and disease. We present Fiber-seq inferred regulatory elements (FIRE) and show that FIRE provides a more comprehensive and quantitative snapshot of the accessible chromatin landscape across the 6 Gbp diploid human genome, overcoming previously unrecognized biases in existing regulatory element catalogs. title: Accurate detection of sub-1% frequency somatic mutations by whole-genome sequencing.
abstract: Continuous advances in read accuracy have positioned bulk whole-genome sequencing as a promising approach for somatic mutation discovery in research and clinical settings, but its utility for detecting low-frequency mutations in high-coverage data has not been thoroughly assessed. We utilized an experimental design featuring (1) primary human fibroblasts with naturally occurring mutations and expanded subclonal populations, (2) induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines corresponding to subclones, and (3) additional iPSC lines originating from other fibroblasts from the same donor, enabling comprehensive evaluation of mutation detection across analytical methods and sequencing depths. Mutations discovered in iPSC lines defined positive control mutations ranging from 0.1% to 25% variant allele fraction (VAF) and negative (i.e., absent) control mutations in fibroblasts. Using the negative controls, we determined PacBio and AVITI as the most accurate sequencing platforms in "easy" (i.e., reliably accessible by short reads) and "non-easy" genomic regions, respectively. AVITI was also the most accurate for indel sequencing. We benchmarked mutation detection in fibroblasts in "easy" regions using ∼1,360× Illumina short-read data for mutation discovery and combined ∼600× PacBio and AVITI data for confirmation. Our analyses demonstrated accurate and specific detection of point mutations below 1% VAF and non-homopolymer indels down to 1% VAF. Homopolymer indels could be reliably detected only at VAF >3%. Mutation detection was degraded in postmortem samples, for which we provide recommendations for additional filtering and data-quality assessment. llm_summary: Researchers evaluated whether whole-genome sequencing could accurately detect somatic mutations (genetic changes occurring in some cells but not others) present at very low frequencies, which is important for understanding disease development and aging in clinical and research settings. The study used primary human fibroblasts with naturally occurring mutations and induced pluripotent stem cell lines to create positive control mutations ranging from 0.1% to 25% variant allele fraction (the proportion of DNA copies carrying a mutation) and negative controls to benchmark different sequencing platforms and methods. The analysis demonstrated that PacBio sequencing was most accurate in easily accessible genomic regions while AVITI sequencing performed best in difficult regions and for detecting small insertions and deletions, with combined high-coverage data enabling reliable detection of point mutations below 1% variant allele fraction and small insertions/deletions at 1% variant allele fraction. The findings suggest that modern sequencing technologies can identify very rare somatic mutations when sufficient sequencing depth is applied, though homopolymer indels (repetitive DNA sequences) required higher frequencies of at least 3% for reliable detection. The researchers noted that mutation detection was degraded in postmortem samples.
