title: A proliferation score defined by PCLI-anchored transcriptomics predicts outcomes in multiple myeloma.
abstract: Cell proliferation is a fundamental driver of disease aggressiveness in multiple myeloma (MM); however, transcriptional programs underpinning proliferative capacity remain incompletely defined. Using Affymetrix microarray data from 136 Mayo Clinic patients with MM with paired plasma cell labeling index (PCLI), we performed a differential expression analysis to identify genes consistently associated with proliferative activity. These genes were subsequently incorporated into the development of a prognostic model using baseline RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) profiles in purified CD138+ cells from 656 patients in the CoMMpass cohort, in which an elastic net-based Cox model yielded an 8-gene-based proliferation score (GPS). Differential expression analysis identified 108 proliferation-associated genes, and the resulting 8-gene GPS (CHEK1, EXO1, MCM4, TK1, KIF14, SEPTIN11, PHF19, and HMGB3) formed a highly connected biological network enriched for DNA damage response and cell cycle regulation. CHEK1, TK1, EXO1, and MCM4 were mapped in a large network with CHEK1 as the hub gene. In the CoMMpass data set, on dividing the GPS score by the median, the high-GPS group (n = 328) had a median overall survival (OS) of 63.6 months (95% confidence interval, 56.5-76.7), whereas the low-GPS group (n = 328) had a median OS of 106.1 months (P < .001). Similarly, in another Mayo Clinic RNA-seq cohort, high-GPS group (n = 12) demonstrated worse survival (median OS, 39.2 vs 157.1 months for the low-GPS group; P = .03). title: Circulating Nephrin Antibodies and Post-Transplant Recurrence of Diffuse Podocytopathies: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Recurrence of diffuse podocytopathy (DP), primarily focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and minimal change disease, after kidney transplantation threatens allograft survival. Circulating nephrin autoantibodies have been linked to disease activity, but posttransplant evidence remains limited. We performed a systematic review with patient-level data extraction, including kidney transplant recipients with DP as their native kidney disease from studies reporting serum nephrin antibody testing and posttransplant outcomes. Four studies including 63 recipients (23 pediatric and 40 adult) with DP were included, comprising 53 focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, 8 minimal change disease, and 2 steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome cases. Nephrin antibodies were detected in 22 of 62 tested recipients (36%), either before transplantation or during posttransplant recurrence, including one patient in whom antibodies were detected 9 years after transplantation. Recurrence occurred in 34 of 63 recipients (54%), including 20 of 22 (91%) antibody-positive patients. Antibody positivity was strongly associated with recurrence (OR 20.8; 95% CI, 4.2-102.6; P < 0.001), with sensitivity of 61%, specificity of 93%, positive predictive value of 91%, and negative predictive value of 68%. Antibody titers correlated with disease activity and declined with remission. Nephrin autoantibodies are associated with posttransplant recurrence of DP and may inform pretransplant risk stratification and posttransplant monitoring. Standardized assays and larger validation studies are needed.© 2026 The Authors.

llm_summary: Researchers reviewed studies examining whether antibodies against a kidney protein called nephrin could predict disease recurrence in transplant patients who had podocytopathy, a condition affecting kidney filtering cells. They found that patients with these antibodies were much more likely to experience disease recurrence after transplantation, with the antibodies present in 91% of patients whose disease came back. However, larger standardized studies are needed to confirm these findings and establish whether testing for these antibodies could help doctors predict which transplant patients face the highest risk.

The analysis included 63 recipients (23 pediatric, 40 adult) from four studies, with nephrin antibodies detected in 22 of 62 tested patients (36%) either before transplantation or during posttransplant follow-up. Nephrin antibody titers correlated with disease activity and declined with remission, and antibodies were detected up to 9 years after transplant.

title: A Pilot Study to Describe Symptomatic Hyperammonemia Secondary to Recombinant Erwinia Asparaginase.
abstract: Asparaginase therapy is essential for the treatment of pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (ALL/LLy). For patients who develop hypersensitivity to a first-line Escherichia coli (E. coli)-derived product, the standard of care is to transition to an Erwinia-derived product. Given that all asparaginase products exert their antileukemic effects by enzymatically breaking down asparagine to aspartic acid and ammonia, elevations in ammonia levels are anticipated during asparaginase treatment. However, symptomatic hyperammonemia is not expected. Recombinant Erwinia asparaginase is relatively new to the market, and there have been several case reports of symptomatic hyperammonemia with this specific formulation.The primary objective of this prospective study was to establish the incidence of symptomatic hyperammonemia secondary to recombinant Erwinia asparaginase and to determine if a larger, multicenter trial was warranted. Additional objectives included identifying potential risk factors for symptomatic hyperammonemia.This single-center, prospective trial received institutional review board approval. Funding was provided by the Mayo Clinic Clinical and Translational Science Award (grant number: UL1TR002377) and the Mayo Clinic Department of Pharmacy. All patients treated by the pediatric hematology/oncology team at our institution who were receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase were eligible. Patients were excluded if they were less than 1 year of age at study entry. Enrolled participants had a baseline plasma ammonia level obtained, followed by twice weekly ammonia levels while receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase. Aside from baseline, all ammonia levels were trough levels measured either 48 h or 72 h after the previous dose.Five patients were included, three of whom were male (60%). Three patients had T-cell ALL (60%), one patient had B-cell ALL (20%), and one patient had infantile B-cell ALL (20%). The median age was 5 years (range 1-14). Two patients were followed for two courses of recombinant Erwinia asparaginase, and the remaining patients were followed for a single course. Median baseline plasma ammonia level was 12 μmol/L. Median ammonia level while receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase was 146 μmol/L. Three patients (60%) developed symptomatic hyperammonemia with a median ammonia level of 174 μmol/L (range 108-343). The reported symptoms were nausea (100%), fatigue (66.7%), and decreased appetite (33.3%). The remaining two patients experienced asymptomatic hyperammonemia with a median ammonia level of 125 μmol/L (range 55-304).Based on our small cohort, symptomatic hyperammonemia may be a common adverse effect for patients receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase. Evaluating plasma ammonia levels appears reasonable in patients who are experiencing nausea or other symptoms of hyperammonemia. Additional studies are warranted to further characterize this toxicity.© 2026 ACCP Foundation, Ltd.

llm_summary: Researchers studied whether a cancer drug called recombinant Erwinia asparaginase, used to treat childhood leukemia, causes dangerously high ammonia levels in the blood that make patients feel sick. In their small study of five children, three developed symptomatic high ammonia levels with nausea and fatigue, suggesting this side effect may be more common than previously recognized. The researchers concluded that checking ammonia levels in patients receiving this drug who feel sick seems reasonable, though larger studies are needed to confirm their findings.
llm_summary_expert: This single-center prospective pilot study enrolled five pediatric patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia or lymphoma receiving recombinant Erwinia asparaginase, with baseline and twice-weekly trough plasma ammonia levels measured during treatment courses. The median baseline ammonia level was 12 μmol/L, which increased to a median of 146 μmol/L during recombinant Erwinia asparaginase therapy. Three patients (60%) developed symptomatic hyperammonemia with a median ammonia level of 174 μmol/L, presenting with nausea (100%), fatigue (66.7%), and decreased appetite (33.3%), while two patients experienced asymptomatic hyperammonemia with a median level of 125 μmol/L. The findings suggest that symptomatic hyperammonemia may be a common adverse effect associated with recombinant Erwinia asparaginase, and plasma ammonia monitoring appears reasonable in patients experiencing relevant symptoms. The small sample size and single-center design limit generalizability and warrant larger multicenter trials to further characterize this potential toxicity.

title: Vascular Abnormalities in the Hand and Wrist: State-of-the-Art Multimodality Imaging.
abstract: Vascular abnormalities are less common in the hand and wrist than in the lower extremities but can result in significant morbidity if unrecognized or untreated. The unique vascular architecture of the hand and wrist, with a dense network of arterial anastomoses, confers resilience to ischemia, but the superficial location makes them vulnerable to trauma and occupational injury. The authors describe and illustrate a comprehensive multimodality imaging approach to the diagnosis and evaluation of vascular abnormalities of the hand and wrist. They begin with an overview of vascular anatomy and normal variants, including a persistent median artery. Multimodality imaging, including US, CT angiography, MR angiography, and digital subtraction angiography, is reviewed with a focus on strengths, limitations, and clinical utility. Dynamic imaging techniques and photon-counting CT are highlighted for their evolving roles. A wide spectrum of vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, trauma, iatrogenic injury, embolism, hypothenar hammer syndrome, hand-arm vibration syndrome, vasculitis, and frostbite, as well as their imaging appearances, are discussed. Vascular anomalies, including vascular malformations and vascular neoplasms, are also reviewed. The role of imaging in hand transplantation is addressed. The authors provide a framework for recognizing vascular diseases in the hand and wrist and selecting the appropriate imaging modality. Familiarity with vascular anatomy, imaging findings, and clinical context is essential for timely diagnosis, guiding management, and preserving limb function.©RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.

title: GABAergic Network Dysregulation in Alcohol Use Disorder: Receptor-Transporter Interactions Driving the Transition From Goal-Directed to Compulsive Behaviour.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is characterized by a shift from controlled, goal-directed drinking to compulsive, habitual alcohol (a.k.a. ethanol) seeking, even in the face of negative outcomes. This transition is closely associated with alterations in cortico-striatal circuitry and dysregulated GABAergic signalling, both of which drive the progression from flexible control to compulsive behaviour. Acute alcohol exposure enhances GABAergic inhibition, primarily by increasing presynaptic GABA release. Chronic exposure leads to compensatory neuroadaptations, such as subunit reorganization, receptor internalization and diminished GABA receptor sensitivity. While these neuroadaptations alter receptor-mediated GABAergic signalling during dependence and withdrawal, they also alter dopaminergic regulation and further reinforce alcohol-seeking behaviour. Beyond receptor-level adaptations, impaired GABA clearance, especially through the astrocytic transporter GAT3, plays a crucial role in regulating extracellular GABA concentrations and tonic inhibition. This effect is particularly evident within the dorsal striatum, where elevated tonic GABA shifts control from flexible, goal-directed action towards rigid, habitual responding by altering the balance between the dorsomedial and dorsolateral subregions. Consistent with these mechanistic insights, animal and human studies demonstrate that reduced GAT3 expression is associated with compulsive alcohol use and impaired reward-related behaviour, reinforcing impaired GABA clearance as a central mechanism in this behavioural shift. Taken together, these lines of evidence validate a central therapeutic model, namely, that targeting altered tonic inhibition and impaired GABA clearance in AUD could address the inhibitory dysfunction that sustains the disorder. Overall, this work supports a unifying model in which receptor adaptations and disrupted GABA removal maintain altered inhibitory tone, driving maladaptive circuit function and contributing to the persistence of AUD.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: This review examines how alcohol use disorder develops when the brain's inhibitory control system becomes dysregulated, particularly through changes in GABA, a chemical messenger that normally suppresses excessive behavior. Chronic alcohol exposure causes the brain to adapt by reducing its sensitivity to GABA and impairing the removal of GABA from brain regions involved in decision-making, which shifts drinking from controlled to compulsive. These findings suggest that therapies targeting GABA clearance and inhibitory function could potentially help restore behavioral control in people with alcohol use disorder.

Chronic alcohol exposure triggers compensatory neuroadaptations including GABA receptor subunit reorganization, receptor internalization, and diminished receptor sensitivity, which alter both GABAergic and dopaminergic regulation to reinforce alcohol-seeking behavior. Impaired GABA clearance through the astrocytic transporter GAT3 plays a critical role in elevating extracellular GABA concentrations and tonic inhibition, particularly in the dorsal striatum where increased tonic GABA shifts behavioral control from flexible, goal-directed actions toward rigid, habitual responding. Animal and human studies demonstrate that reduced GAT3 expression is associated with compulsive alcohol use and impaired reward-related behavior, supporting impaired GABA clearance as a central mechanism in this behavioral transition. The authors propose that therapeutic targeting of altered tonic inhibition and impaired GABA clearance could address the inhibitory dysfunction that sustains alcohol use disorder by restoring normal circuit.

title: Living Liver Donors With Obesity and Metabolic Risk: Review and Guidance on Donor Triage and Care.
abstract: With the increasing prevalence of obesity in the United States, potential living liver donors (LLDs) are similarly impacted. Historically, LLDs with obesity are deemed too high risk for donation due to concern for hepatic steatosis (HS) or post-surgical complications. Evolving data show that obesity is not the absolute indicator of HS and metabolic risk. Instead, distribution of fat in the visceral area as well as body composition drive the risk for metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Prior practice patterns of denial of obese LLDs with metabolic risk require a change in mindset from the liver transplant community with a thoughtful, individualized risk assessment of all LLDs. By losing weight utilizing various dietary and procedural strategies, these "gray zone" LLDs improve their metabolic risk profile and can move into a low risk "green zone", thus expanding the donor pool. Little data exist whether "gray zone" LLDs who succeed in weight loss have long-term consequences to their own health if they regain their weight or the clinical impact on their LDLT recipients. Ethical and financial questions remain as to the LDLT centers' direct responsibility to maintaining donor health. Future studies evaluating interventions and outcomes are needed.© 2026 John Wiley & Sons A/S. Published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

llm_summary: Researchers reviewed how obesity affects living liver donors and found that obesity alone does not necessarily make someone too risky to donate, since the location of body fat and overall body composition matter more for liver health. Donors classified as higher risk can potentially move to lower risk categories through weight loss using diet and other strategies, which could expand the available donor pool. However, important questions remain about whether donors who lose weight and then regain it experience long-term health problems and how this affects transplant recipients.
llm_summary_expert: This review examines the evaluation and management of living liver donors with obesity and metabolic risk, challenging the historical practice of categorically excluding obese donors based solely on body mass index. The authors argue that visceral fat distribution and body composition, rather than obesity alone, are the primary drivers of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and post-surgical complications in potential donors. The paper proposes an individualized risk assessment approach that stratifies donors into risk categories, with "gray zone" donors potentially improving their metabolic profile through weight loss interventions and dietary or procedural strategies to transition into a low-risk "green zone. " This approach could expand the living donor liver transplant pool by identifying suitable candidates previously denied based on obesity status alone. The authors identify critical gaps in knowledge regarding long-term health consequences for donors who lose weight preoperatively but regain it postoperatively, as well as the clinical impact on recipients, and call for future studies to evaluate interventions and outcomes alongside clarification of transplant centers' ethical and financial responsibilities for donor health maintenance.

title: Characterizing bone metastases and skeletal-related events in patients with well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms utilizing 68Gallium-DOTATATE positron emission tomography.
abstract: Tumors of neuroendocrine origin are a heterogenous group of related neoplasms which can arise from anywhere in the body. Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) are categorized by site of origin, differentiation status and grade (Ki-67 expression and/or mitotic rate), with significant prognostic variability accordingly. Historically, the prevalence of bone metastasis is reported to be 6%-12% based on "first generation" (i.e., 111Indium pentetreotide [Octreoscan®]) somatostatin receptor imaging (SSRI). We conducted a retrospective cohort study including patients with well-differentiated NENs to determine the clinical and imaging characteristics of osseous metastases when evaluated with higher-sensitivity 68Gallium-DOTATATE positron emission tomography (PET) scans, as well as determining fracture prevalence in selected sub-cohorts. We also developed a risk score analysis to assess risk of fracture in this cohort. Four hundred twenty-four patients were identified for inclusion. The median age was 61 years. Most patients were asymptomatic (64%), had sclerotic lesions (77%), Krenning 4 (71%), and had >3 sites (69%) of osseous disease. A high proportion of patients had osseous metastases at sites with high risk for fracture, including vertebra (82%), pelvis (63%), and peri-trochanteric femur (34%). Fifty-seven patients (13%) in the entire cohort suffered a fracture. Fracture prevalence was significantly lower in small bowel neuroendocrine tumors (NETs, 7%) and Grades 1 and 2 disease (8% and 9%, respectively), with higher prevalence in pancreatic NETs, paragangliomas/pheochromocytomas, lung carcinoid, and Grade 3 disease (≥20% for each; p-values <.05). Our study showed that the rate of osseous metastatic disease approximates 20% in well-differentiated NENs. Most bone metastases are asymptomatic and the risk of fracture is variable based on the primary site of disease and tumor grade. Our novel risk score analysis for fracture was designed to assist clinician decision making as to management of bone metastasis in this patient population.© 2026 The Author(s). title: Development of the Children's Oncology Group long-term follow-up guideline for cancer genetics evaluation in childhood cancer survivors.
abstract: Up to 12% of childhood cancer survivors have an underlying cancer predisposition syndrome (CPS). As a result, these childhood cancer survivors are at increased risk for developing and succumbing to subsequent malignant neoplasms. Identifying childhood cancer survivors with CPS is essential to improving overall outcomes by informing tailored approaches to cancer screening, treatment, and, for some, risk-reducing interventions. Despite these potential benefits, it is often unclear which childhood cancer survivors warrant referral for genetic counselling and germline genetic testing. Using an evidence-based approach, a standardised guideline for referral for cancer genetics evaluation of childhood cancer survivors at high risk of having a CPS was developed and incorporated into the Children's Oncology Group Long-Term Follow-Up Guidelines for Survivors of Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancers. This Policy Review details the importance, development, and anticipated impact of this new guideline. Raising awareness of this guideline is crucial to enhancing the integration of genetics into survivorship care and improving health outcomes for childhood cancer survivors with CPS.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. title: Differential contributions of CO2 and blood pressure to cerebral macro- and microvascular reactivity in healthy adults.
abstract: Cerebrovascular reactivity to CO2 (CVR-CO2) is widely used to assess cerebrovascular function, yet it remains unclear how changes in upstream arterial inflow and downstream microvascular oxygenation are coupled during CO2 perturbations, and how concurrent blood pressure (BP) changes modulate these responses. We aimed to quantify macro- and microvascular CVR-CO2 while disentangling the relative and independent contributions of BP and CO2 during hypo- and hypercapnic stimuli. In 41 healthy adults, including 21 female participants, macrovascular blood flow velocity (CBFV; transcranial Doppler) and microvascular oxygenation (oxyhemoglobin; near-infrared spectroscopy) were recorded during hyperventilation-induced hypocapnia and rebreathing-induced hypercapnia. Hypocapnic reactivity was assessed using linear regression of changes in end-tidal CO2 and BP, while hypercapnic responses were analyzed breath-by-breath using linear mixed-effects models. During hypocapnia, CO2 was the primary driver of both macrovascular and microvascular responses, with negligible BP contributions and only modest macro- and micro-CVR-CO2 correlations. In contrast, during hypercapnia, while CO2 remained dominant, macro- and micro-CVR-CO2 correlations were absent; BP contributed proportionally more to macrovascular than to microvascular responses. These findings indicate that BP independently influences CVR-CO2 during hypercapnia and that microvascular responses to CO2 diverge from upstream arterial inflow. Recognizing these differential vascular responses to CO2 improves interpretations of CVR-CO2 metrics and likely informs individualized assessment of cerebrovascular function.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study indicates that cerebrovascular reactivity to CO2 (CVR-CO2) differs between the macro- and microcirculation during both hypocapnia and hypercapnia and that relative contributions of CO2 and blood pressure to these responses differ between vascular compartments during hypercapnia. These findings highlight the importance of considering compartment-specific regulatory mechanisms when interpreting CVR-CO2.

llm_summary: Researchers studied how blood vessels in the brain respond to changes in carbon dioxide levels and blood pressure in 41 healthy adults by measuring blood flow in large vessels and oxygen levels in tiny vessels during controlled breathing exercises. They found that carbon dioxide was the main driver of vessel responses during low carbon dioxide conditions, but during high carbon dioxide conditions, blood pressure also played a significant independent role, and small vessels responded differently than large vessels. These findings suggest that doctors should consider different parts of the brain's circulation separately when assessing how well blood vessels are functioning.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers examined cerebrovascular reactivity to CO2 (CVR-CO2) in 41 healthy adults (21 female) by measuring macrovascular blood flow velocity via transcranial Doppler and microvascular oxygenation via near-infrared spectroscopy during hyperventilation-induced hypocapnia and rebreathing-induced hypercapnia. During hypocapnia, CO2 was the primary driver of both macrovascular and microvascular responses with negligible blood pressure contributions, whereas macro- and micro-CVR-CO2 correlations were only modest. During hypercapnia, CO2 remained dominant but macro- and micro-CVR-CO2 correlations were absent, and blood pressure contributed proportionally more to macrovascular than to microvascular responses. These findings indicate that blood pressure independently influences CVR-CO2 during hypercapnia and that microvascular responses to CO2 diverge from upstream arterial inflow. title: Blood- and Liver Stiffness-Based Non-Invasive Tests for Clinically Significant Portal Hypertension in Patients With cACLD and HCC.
abstract: The applicability of non-invasive tests (NITs) for clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is controversial. We performed a head-to-head comparison of various NITs for CSPH and evaluated rule-in/-out criteria.We conducted a retrospective study including 283 patients with HCC undergoing hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) measurement at the Vienna Hepatic Haemodynamic Lab with available, same-day data on NITs (i.e., liver stiffness measurement [LSM], platelet count [PLT], von Willebrand factor antigen [VWF:Ag], and the ratio of VWF:Ag and PLT [VITRO]). For the subsequent analysis, we focused on patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD).Among 164 patients with cACLD, most were BCLC 0/A (50.6%) and CSPH prevalence was 46.3%, the median LSM was 20.0 kPa (IQR: 13.3-37.9), and mean VWF:Ag/VITRO was 266 ± 119%/2.30 ± 1.81. The VITRO score yielded the highest discriminative ability to detect CSPH (AUROC: 0.834), followed by ANTICIPATE ± NASH (AUROC: 0.822), PLT (AUROC: 0.803), LSM (AUROC: 0.779), and VWF:Ag (AUROC: 0.707). The application of the Baveno VII criterium (LSM ≤ 15 kPa & PLT ≥ 150G/L) and the VITRO score (≤ 1.0) individually showed an excellent performance for ruling-out CSPH (sensitivities: ≥ 95%, NPV: 100%/87.9%). For ruling-in CSPH by individual criteria, the VITRO score provided the highest PPV (≥ 2.5, specificity/PPV: 89.8%/83.0%), followed by the Baveno VII criteria (specificity/PPV: 81.8%/74.6%). When sequentially applying Baveno VII criteria and VITRO, the grey zone could be significantly reduced to 16% (sensitivity/NPV: 94.7%/92.2%; specificity/PPV: 73.9%/84.4%).The discriminative ability in patients with cACLD and HCC was comparable to patients without HCC. However, PPVs of established criteria were < 90%, which may be explained by the comparatively low prevalence of CSPH in this context.© 2026 The Author(s). llm_summary: Researchers compared different blood and liver stiffness tests to detect dangerous high blood pressure in the liver among patients with liver cancer and advanced liver disease. The VITRO score, which measures two blood proteins, performed best at identifying patients with this condition, with a success rate of about 83 percent when used to confirm the diagnosis. However, the tests were less reliable for confirming the condition than for ruling it out, partly because fewer patients in this group actually had the dangerous pressure.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers conducted a retrospective study of 164 patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma who underwent hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement with simultaneous assessment of non-invasive tests including liver stiffness measurement, platelet count, von Willebrand factor antigen, and the VITRO score. The VITRO score demonstrated the highest discriminative ability for detecting clinically significant portal hypertension with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.834, followed by ANTICIPATE ± NASH (0.822), platelet count (0.803), liver stiffness measurement (0.779), and von Willebrand factor antigen (0.707). Sequential application of Baveno VII criteria and the VITRO score reduced the indeterminate grey zone to 16% while maintaining sensitivity and negative predictive value of 94.7% and 92.2% for ruling out clinically significant portal hypertension. Positive predictive values for ruling in clinically significant portal hypertension remained below 90% for established criteria, with the VITRO score providing the highest positive predictive value of 83.

title: Efficiently harvesting low-energy photons from silicon photon counting detectors.
abstract: X-rays incident on silicon photon counting detectors (Si PCDs) may undergo Compton scattering and deposit only a few keV of energy into the sensor. These events are difficult to distinguish from electronic noise. Prior to reconstruction, the scanner must solve a hybrid estimation problem to determine attenuation, in which the lowest energy bin is corrupted by false counts, but the upper energy bins are essentially immune to electronic noise.To efficiently estimate attenuation in this hybrid scenario. Prior authors have considered attenuation estimation with PCDs that are fully immune to electronic noise, or in energy-integrating detectors that include electronic noise, but the optimal estimator in the hybrid scenario remains unknown. The purpose of this work is to design such an attenuation estimator that reduces bias and variance in Si-PCD CT images.We propose to use convex optimization to build a 2D-lookup table that maps counts using the lowest energy bin (containing false counts) and the upper bins (all counts grouped together as a single bin, free of false counts) to the best estimated object attenuation. The energy thresholds of the Si PCD were selected to be 6 and 10 keV using assumptions from the literature. In the regime of interest, counts are scarce, so both false counts and true counts were modeled as Poisson. Our proposed estimator was compared with three reference estimators: naive logarithm estimator and modified logarithm estimators based on Li et al. (IEEE Trans Med Img 2023) and Bushe et al. (Phys Med Biol 2023). The reference estimators were applied using either both lowest and upper bins, or using upper bins only. 20-, 30- and 40- cm water phantoms, containing two 2.6-cm bone-like inserts, were tested in simulation. We assumed a technique of 120 kVp and 833 mA without mA modulation. To avoid confounding artifacts from beam hardening, the bone-like inserts were modeled as being water-equivalent in atomic number but high density, and a water beam hardening correction was used.The proposed estimator achieved zero average bias and the lowest variance across all phantom sizes when compared to the reference estimators. When using both energy bins for the 30-cm phantom, the logarithm, Li's, and Bushe's estimators had biases of 4, 1, and 1 HU and variances that were 7%, 5%, and 5% higher than the proposed method, respectively, in the area between the two inserts. For the 40-cm phantom, their biases increased to over 20 HU. Conversely, when using only the upper energy bins for the 30-cm phantom, the logarithm, Li's, and Bushe's estimators had biases of 4, 0, and 0 HU but with significant increase in variance to 17%, 14%, and 14% higher than our estimator, respectively, and still produced bias on the 40-cm phantom.For Si PCDs, setting the lowest energy threshold low enough to detect at least some false counts in combination with our proposed attenuation estimator can improve dose efficiency for non-spectral imaging tasks.© 2026 American Association of Physicists in Medicine.

llm_summary: Researchers developed a new method to improve X-ray imaging with silicon detectors that struggle to distinguish real signals from electronic noise in the lowest energy range. Their proposed approach used mathematical optimization to better estimate tissue density by combining information from both noisy and clean energy measurements, achieving zero average bias and lower variance than existing methods. This technique could allow hospitals to use lower radiation doses while maintaining image quality in standard X-ray CT scans.
llm_summary_expert: Researchers developed a convex optimization-based attenuation estimator for silicon photon counting detectors (Si PCDs) that uses a two-dimensional lookup table mapping counts from low-energy bins (contaminated by electronic noise) and upper-energy bins (noise-free) to estimated object attenuation. The proposed method was evaluated against three reference estimators (naive logarithm, Li et al. , and Bushe et al. ) using simulated CT scans of 20-, 30-, and 40-cm water phantoms with bone-like inserts at 120 kVp. The proposed estimator achieved zero average bias and the lowest variance across all phantom sizes, with reference estimators showing biases up to 20 Hounsfield units and variances 5-17% higher on the 30-cm phantom depending on which energy bins were used.

title: The Pros & Cons of Measuring Plasma Ammonia in the Management of Patients With Cirrhosis: An ISHEN Debate.
abstract: Ammonia is a nitrogenous molecule which is primarily generated in the gastrointestinal tract. The neurotoxicity of ammonia plays a critical role in the liver's regulation of circulating ammonia levels. In liver disease, an increase in blood ammonia has been long implicated in the pathogenesis of hepatic encephalopathy (HE), a neurological complication of liver disease. However, the clinical value of measuring plasma ammonia in patients with cirrhosis remains controversial. This dilemma was the subject of a debate held at the International Society of Hepatic Encephalopathy and Nitrogen Metabolism (ISHEN) meeting in St-Paulin, Québec, Canada in October 2025. This review illustrates the pros & cons of measuring plasma ammonia in the management of patients with cirrhosis.© 2026 The Author(s). Liver International published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

llm_summary: Ammonia, a toxic substance produced in the digestive tract, has long been suspected of causing hepatic encephalopathy, a brain disorder in patients with severe liver disease. Researchers examined whether measuring blood ammonia levels is actually useful for managing cirrhosis patients, debating the practical benefits and limitations of this test. The review presents both arguments for and against ammonia measurement, highlighting that despite ammonia's suspected role in brain damage, the clinical value of testing remains uncertain and controversial.
llm_summary_expert: Ammonia is a nitrogenous molecule generated primarily in the gastrointestinal tract whose neurotoxicity is implicated in hepatic encephalopathy, a neurological complication of cirrhosis. Blood ammonia elevation has long been associated with the pathogenesis of hepatic encephalopathy in patients with liver disease, though the clinical utility of measuring plasma ammonia in cirrhotic patients remains contested. The International Society of Hepatic Encephalopathy and Nitrogen Metabolism convened a debate at their October 2025 meeting in St-Paulin, Québec, Canada to examine this clinical controversy. This review presents arguments both supporting and opposing the measurement of plasma ammonia in the management of cirrhotic patients. The abstract does not report specific quantitative findings or resolution of the debate, instead framing the paper as a presentation of competing perspectives on ammonia measurement utility.

title: Results from the VANISH study: A prospective multicenter study validating a single-nucleotide polymorphism-based noninvasive prenatal test to assess aneuploidy risk in surviving twins of vanishing twin pregnancies.
abstract: To develop and validate a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based noninvasive prenatal cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening algorithm capable of identifying the cfDNA signal of the living fetus in vanishing twin (VT) pregnancies and assessing that twin's aneuploidy risk.Prospective study enrolling participants ≥18 years old at ≥9 weeks' gestation with an ultrasound-confirmed VT at 21 US sites (August 2021 to August 2023). The study protocol specified SNP-based cfDNA screening at enrollment and at two additional 3-week intervals. Neonatal buccal swabs evaluated the SNP profile of the living fetus. Cases lost to follow-up and with missing samples were excluded. Using SNP-based technology, an algorithm to identify the living fetus was developed based on the number of fetoplacental cfDNA signals and individual fetal fraction measurements. Concordance between cfDNA in maternal plasma and newborn buccal-swab SNP profiles was used to validate the algorithm in correctly identifying the living fetus. Common aneuploidies and fetal sex were determined for the living fetus.Of 136 participants enrolled, 106 met criteria for the final analysis; 45 for development and 61 for validation. In the validation cohort, median gestational age was 10.7 weeks (range: 8.0-16.1 weeks) at ultrasound diagnosis of a VT. In 93.4% of validation cases, the algorithm identified the living fetus and gave an aneuploidy result; 90.2% within the first two blood draws. At the time the living fetus was identified, 39 samples had two fetoplacental signals and 18 had one. Aneuploidy results included 56 low-risk and one high-risk result for trisomy 21. Neonatal buccal swabs confirmed that the VT algorithm correctly identified the living twin and gave a correct aneuploidy result in 57/57 cases (100%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 93.5%, 100.0%). Among 29 participants with all three blood draws and two fetoplacental signals at enrollment, two signals persisted in 93.1% at the second blood draw and 72.4% at the third.The SNP-based algorithm accurately identified the living fetus in VT pregnancies in this small study. Aneuploidy risk assessment was validated in all cases where the cfDNA signal for the living twin was identified, though these findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited sample size.ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05004337.© 2026 The Authors. title: Application of Optic Neuritis Diagnostic Criteria in Autoimmune Paraneoplastic CRMP5 Optic Neuropathy and Development of the "CRMP" Score.
abstract: Collapsin response-mediator protein 5 (CRMP5)-IgG is an acknowledged biomarker in the International Consortium on Optic Neuritis (ICON) diagnostic criteria for optic neuritis (ON), but these criteria have not been validated in CRMP5-IgG+ON.We evaluated the ICON and Acute Optic Neuritis Network (ACON) criteria for CRMP5-IgG+ON, using patients with late-onset (age ≥50 years) aquaporin-4-IgG-positive (AQP4-IgG+)-ON or myelin-oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody (MOG-IgG+)-ON for comparison. We developed the "CRMP score," based on typical CRMP5-IgG+ON clinical features, to guide CRMP5 antibody testing in ON.The study included 17 patients with CRMP5-IgG+, 11 with AQP4-IgG+ON, and 13 with MOG-IgG+ON. Application of ICON criteria yielded no "definite ON" and 1 "probable ON" diagnosis among the 17 CRMP5-IgG+ cases, but definite ON diagnoses for 6 of 11 AQP4-IgG+ (55%, p = 0.003) and 7 of 13 MOG-IgG+ cases (54%, p = 0.001). ACON criteria yielded definite ON diagnoses for 2 (12%) CRMP5-IgG+ON, 10 (91%) of the AQP4-IgG+ON, and 13 (100%) of the MOG-IgG+ON (p < 0.001). A CRMP score ≥1 identified CRMP5-IgG+ON with a sensitivity of 88.2% and a specificity of 87.5%.ICON and ACON criteria for ON diagnosis identified only a minority of CRMP5-IgG+ON cases; thus, we developed the "CRMP" score to aid their identification in clinical practice.

title: End-to-end film-based characterization of gated delivery latencies in a spot-scanned synchrotron-based proton therapy system.
abstract: Temporal mismatches between gating signals and beam activation-beam-on and beam-off latencies-in gated particle beam therapy can compromise dose integrity. Yet standardized measurement techniques are lacking, and system-specific characterization, particularly for synchrotron-based proton systems, remains limited.To implement a novel strategy for precise end-to-end gating latency measurements of a spot-scanned proton beam using Gafchromic film.Gating latencies have been measured for a Hitachi ProBeat accelerator equipped with a Varian RPM gating system. EBT4 films were positioned within a stack of acrylic blocks on a QUASAR respiratory motion platform operated with a 1.5 cm amplitude and 12 bpm sinusoidal pattern. A stainless-steel ball bearing (BB), positioned atop the film, facilitated localization. During irradiation, the BB produced a dose shadow on the film that indicated the phantom position. A proton plan consisting of a single 85.3 MeV spot was delivered to isocenter during a single gate-on/off interval initiated near the 25% phase, to maximize phantom velocity. Fifty-one measurements were made with a variety of gating intervals. Beam-on latency and delivery time produced a separation between the BB-shadow and the centroid of the Gaussian proton spot. Spot duration information was extracted from accelerator log files. BB-shadow/spot separation is modeled analytically based on phantom motion enabling the direct calculation of the total beam-on and beam-off latencies. Accelerator latency was measured directly with an oscilloscope, enabling isolation of the relative contributions of the RPM gating system.An average beam-on latency of 142 ± 27  ms is observed for the RPM+ProBeat system for the first gate of a delivery, which includes a known 69 ms beam extraction judgment time for the first proton spot in a spill from the Hitachi synchrotron. The corresponding average beam-off latency is 87 ± 30  ms  . The average gate-on and gate-off latencies of the RPM system are calculated as 72 ± 27  ms  and 81 ± 30  ms  , respectively. The associated average contributions of the accelerator to the beam-on latencies are measured as 69.3 ± 0.2  ms  (first gate in new spill) and 0.53 ± 0.07  ms  (subsequent gates in existing spill) and similarly 6 ± 4  ms  for beam-off latency.A novel, high-precision method for gating-latency measurements has been implemented using film to characterize gating latencies in a spot-scanned particle beam. Commissioning and regular quality assurance methods to precisely characterize the temporal accuracy of a gating system ensure treatment accuracy and will become increasingly vital to consider for higher-frequency applications, such as cardiac gating or FLASH-capable systems.© 2026 The Author(s). title: Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement: Clinical Challenges, Evolving Indications, and Future Directions.
abstract: Mitral regurgitation is a highly prevalent valvular heart disease and, when hemodynamically significant, is associated with adverse outcomes. Despite advances in surgical techniques and catheter-based edge-to-edge repair, a large number of patients remain untreated due to high surgical risk or anatomical limitations. Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) has emerged as a promising therapeutic option for these patients. Over the past 15 years, the TMVR field has substantially progressed, with multiple devices advancing to human clinical evaluation. This review aims to provide an overview of the key milestones in TMVR development, patient selection pathways, and the transition from transapical to transseptal delivery. llm_summary: Mitral regurgitation, a common heart valve disease, affects many patients who cannot undergo surgery or receive other treatments due to high risk or anatomical constraints. Transcatheter mitral valve replacement, a catheter-based procedure performed without open surgery, has emerged as a promising treatment option for these patients over the past 15 years. title: Fingerprinting the polycystic kidney: radiomics of the noncystic parenchyma for earlier ADPKD detection.
abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease risk stratification relies on total kidney volume, a validated marker of cyst burden and progression. Kremer et al.'s pilot study used rapid breath-hold magnetic resonance fingerprinting with radiomics to evaluate noncystic renal parenchyma in children and young adults. Quantitative T1/T2 texture features distinguished autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease from controls independently of total kidney volume, cyst fraction, age, or body size, suggesting early tissue changes. title: Weakly supervised deep learning distinguishes alcohol-associated from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis on H&E whole-slide images.
abstract: Distinguishing alcohol-associated steatohepatitis (ASH) from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is challenging given the absence of pathognomonic differentiators. We developed and evaluated a weakly supervised deep learning model, as a single-institution proof-of-concept study, to test whether routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) of liver biopsies contain sufficient morphological information to predict steatohepatitis etiology at the slide level. A retrospective cohort of 1147 WSIs was assembled (train set: 1007, holdout test set: 140). Models were trained using 5-fold patient-level cross-validation at ×20 and ×40 magnification. Model interpretability was assessed through attention-based clustering with blinded pathologist review of high-attention patches. The ×20 model achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic of 0.86 ± 0.01 on the test set, with balanced accuracy of 0.80. The ×40 model performed comparably. Specificity was high (0.93 at ×20), with an ASH sensitivity of 0.67 at ×20. Fibrosis-stratified showed preserved performance at advanced fibrosis (stage ≥3) with balanced accuracy of 82.5% and ASH sensitivity of 77.4%. Attention-based clustering localized ASH-enriched regions to active injury patterns including Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophilic inflammation, cholestatic change, and pericellular fibrosis, whereas MASH-enriched regions showed steatosis with lower inflammatory activity. Weakly supervised deep learning applied to routine liver H&E WSIs can discriminate ASH from MASH with performance preserved at advanced fibrosis. The comparable performance of ×20 and ×40 magnification, and the alignment of model attention with established histological features, support the use of routine morphology as a decision-support input in cases with incomplete or conflicting clinical histories, particularly when the etiological distinction has the greatest implications for management.© 2026 The Author(s).

title: Survival benefit of chemoradiotherapy in limited-stage mantle cell lymphoma: a National Cancer Database analysis.
abstract: Limited-stage mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) is rare, and optimal management remains undefined because of limited representation in clinical studies. We conducted a large population-based analysis using the National Cancer Database to evaluate overall survival (OS) in patients with Ann Arbor stage I to II MCL diagnosed between 2004 and 2015. Initial treatment was categorized to chemotherapy alone, radiotherapy (RT) alone, or combined chemotherapy plus RT (Chemo+RT), and outcomes were further stratified by stage and era of diagnosis (2004-2009 vs 2010-2015) to account for advances in systemic therapy, such as the adoption of bendamustine-rituximab for frontline therapy and the availability of Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors for relapsed disease. Among 2428 patients included, median OS for the entire cohort was 8.1 years. Chemo+RT was associated with superior OS compared with chemotherapy alone or RT alone (median OS, 11.2 vs 7.4 vs 8.0 years, respectively; P < .001). This survival benefit was observed in both stage I and stage II diseases and in both eras. On multivariable analysis, treatment with chemotherapy alone (hazard ratio [HR], 1.50) or RT alone (HR, 1.33) was independently associated with inferior OS compared with Chemo+RT. In this, to our knowledge, largest real-world analysis of limited-stage MCL to date, combined chemoimmunotherapy and RT was associated with a clinically meaningful survival benefit, including in the modern treatment era. These findings suggest that combined-modality therapy may be preferred for appropriately selected patients with limited-stage MCL.© 2026 American Society of Hematology. Published by Elsevier Inc. title: Reliability of computational versus noncomputational metrics of working memory and episodic memory in serious mental illness.
abstract: Computational models can be used to decompose overall behavior into individual parameters that are designed to isolate specific cognitive and neural processes and provide new information about psychiatric disorders. However, it is not yet clear whether these computational parameters have sufficient reliability to replace traditional noncomputational metrics, especially in severe mental illness. The present study asked whether computational parameters can be as reliable as, or even more reliable than, noncomputational performance metrics in healthy control participants (n = 105) and people with schizophrenia spectrum disorder (n = 72), bipolar disorder (n = 68), and major depressive disorder (n = 76). These participants were tested in working memory and episodic memory paradigms. We applied a computational model that yielded parameters corresponding to memory storage capacity, memory precision, and the rate of attention lapses. We also examined a noncomputational metric of performance, the mean error. Each participant was tested twice, separated by at least 28 days. In most cases, the computational parameters exhibited good-to-excellent split-half and test-retest reliability (>0.80) that was comparable with the reliability of the noncomputational performance metric. In one case, reliability was substantially better for the memory precision parameter than for the noncomputational metric. In another case, reliability for the memory precision parameter was substantially lower but was improved by the use of hierarchical Bayesian estimation. Thus, when applied thoughtfully, parameters derived from computational models can have excellent psychometric properties, providing a reliable means of isolating the factors that underlie individual and group differences in studies of mental illness. title: Approximately 30% of Patients Undergoing Knee Cartilage Biopsy Subsequently Undergo Matrix-Induced Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation at a Mean 4.3-Year Follow-Up.
abstract: To evaluate implantation rates, time to implantation, and predictors of implantation following matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation (MACI) biopsy for knee chondral defects.Patients undergoing MACI biopsy or implantation for symptomatic knee chondral defects from 2017 to 2024 at a single institution were reviewed. At a minimum 1-year follow-up, the decision to proceed with implantation, recurrent symptoms, complications, and reoperations were assessed. Kaplan-Meier analysis estimated time to implantation, and multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of MACI implantation.A total of 208 knees in 202 patients (mean age 28.0 ± 10.9 years, range 11-59) underwent MACI biopsy for 243 chondral defects (patella [38%], femoral condyle [34%], and trochlea [26%]). At a mean follow-up of 4.3 years (range 1.0-8.3), 64 knees (31%) proceeded to second-stage MACI implantation. Among 144 knees not implanted, 87 (60%) reported symptom improvement, and 26 (18%) had persistent symptoms. The remaining 22% did not undergo implantation due to another cartilage procedure, insurance denial, or pending scheduling. Patients who underwent biopsy at the home institution had a shorter time from biopsy to implantation compared with those biopsied at outside institutions (6.1 vs 13.1 months, P = .001). Median time to implantation was 9.4 months (95% confidence level: 7.2-12.2) for home biopsies. Lower body mass index was associated with progression to implantation after adjusting for covariates (odds ratios 0.92, P = .019). Patients implanted within 4 months had larger chondral defects (4.0 vs 3.0 cm2, P = .045). At a mean 4.1-year follow-up, 6 patients (8%) experienced postoperative complications, including 3 (4%) who required revision chondroplasty.MACI biopsy for knee chondral defects resulted in approximately one-third of patients proceeding to MACI implantation, at a median of 9.4 months after biopsy. Lower body mass index was associated with higher likelihood of progression to implantation, larger chondral defects with earlier implantation, and among patients who did not proceed to implantation, approximately 60% reported symptom improvement following concomitant chondroplasty at the time of biopsy.Level IV, retrospective case series.© 2026 the Arthroscopy Association of North America.

title: Reduced Phrenic CMAP Amplitudes in Obesity Despite Preserved Diaphragm Ultrasound Measures.
abstract: Phrenic nerve conduction studies (NCS) are regularly used in the evaluation of neuromuscular respiratory dysfunction; however, the impact of body mass index (BMI) on phrenic compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes remains poorly characterized. We evaluated the relationship between BMI and phrenic CMAP amplitudes in patients without evidence of neuromuscular diaphragmatic dysfunction.We performed a retrospective secondary analysis of patients derived from two previously published cohorts from Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota) and the University of Alberta (Edmonton, Alberta) evaluating diaphragm ultrasound in suspected neuromuscular respiratory insufficiency. Patients without evidence of neuromuscular disease affecting the diaphragm who underwent bilateral phrenic NCS and diaphragm ultrasound were included.Seventy-nine patients met inclusion criteria, including 36 with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2. Median phrenic CMAP amplitudes were significantly lower in patients with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 compared to BMI < 30 kg/m2 (0.25 mV [IQR 0.10-0.38] vs. 0.50 mV [0.30-0.65], p < 0.001). title: The radiographic effect of cage subsidence on neuroforamina after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion.
abstract: Retrospective Cohort Study.The objective of this study is to investigate the effect of cage subsidence on neuroforaminal area after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) utilizing computed tomography (CT).Restoration of disc height via implantation of an interbody device provides an indirect decompression of the cervical neuroforamina. Interbody cage subsidence is a potential postoperative occurrence, but the effect of this on neuroforaminal area has yet to be characterized.A retrospective review was conducted of patients who underwent one- to four-levels of ACDF utilizing an interbody device with anterior plating. Cage subsidence, neuroforaminal area, height and width were measured on CT scans preoperatively and at least 6 months postoperatively. Levels with a cumulative sum of cranial and caudal subsidence greater than 4 mm were classified as severely subsided, while levels with cumulative subsidence less than 4 mm were classified as non-severely subsided.A total of 83 patients (151 levels) were included in this retrospective analysis. Average endplate subsidence was 3.2 ± 1.9 mm. Non-severely subsided levels demonstrated a greater perioperative increase in neuroforaminal area (7.9 vs 2.1 mm2, p < 0.001), neuroforaminal height (1.1 vs 0.4 mm, p < 0.001) and neuroforaminal width (0.7 vs 0.1 mm, p < 0.001) compared to severely subsided levels. Interbody subsidence significantly predicted a decreased change in neuroforaminal height, width and area (p < 0.001). Severe subsidence was associated with an increased rate of pseudarthrosis, but similar reoperation rates and recurrent neurologic deficits between the two groups.Severe subsidence of interbody cages after an ACDF was associated with a decreased perioperative change in neuroforaminal dimensions. This decrease in the size of the neuroforamen may reduce the effect of indirect decompression of the nerve root.Published by Elsevier Ltd.

title: reFLASH: a proof-of-concept meta-analytic framework to validate surrogate endpoints in the absence of randomized clinical trial data.
abstract: Within a meta-analytic framework, validating surrogate endpoints traditionally requires individual patient data (IPD) from multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs). This is rarely feasible in rare and indolent diseases. We propose a proof-of-concept strategy that creates synthetic comparative evidence from multiple single-arm trials to enable trial-level surrogacy assessment.Using IPD from 12 follicular lymphoma RCTs (FLASH; 3996 patients), we decoupled each trial's randomized arms into 24 single-arm trials and re-paired them into 12 artificial trials (reFLASH1) via prespecified rules (therapeutic era, randomization timing, and clinical comparability). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to create "comparable" populations between two arms nested within each pseudo trial, to mimic randomization. Marginal treatment effects were estimated using weighted logistic regression for complete response at 30 months (CR30) (odds ratios, OR) and weighted Cox models for progression-free survival (PFS) (hazard ratios, HR). Trial-level surrogacy between CR30 and PFS was quantified using a bivariate mixed-effects (BvME) model and a weighted least squares (WLS) regression model. Robustness was evaluated with leave-one-out (LOO) analyses. A second pairing strategy (reFLASH2) served as a sensitivity analysis. Original FLASH trials (n = 12) were re-analyzed as benchmark.In reFLASH1, pseudo-trials demonstrated substantial variability in treatment effects (ORs 0.10-15.93; HRs 0.20-2.90), while trial-level surrogacy remained robust, with R2_BvME = 0.769 (95% CI, 0.529-1.000) and R2_WLS = 0.769 (95% CI, 0.341-0.926), meeting predefined acceptability thresholds. In reFLASH2, which applied an alternative arm-matching algorithm, treatment effect ranges were similar (ORs 0.08-8.20; HRs 0.24-6.17), and surrogacy estimates were virtually unchanged (R2_BvME = 0.766; 95% CI, 0.525-1.00; R2_WLS = 0.766; 95% CI, 0.336-0.925). LOO analyses generally kept R2 > 0.70, indicating robustness.Creating artificial comparative trials from single-arm cohorts, combined with IPTW, recovered high trial-level surrogacy between CR30 and PFS, though lower than the RCT-based benchmark obtained under the same analytical framework. While not a substitute for randomization and subject to residual confounding and pairing choices, the reFLASH concept offers a pragmatic pathway to surrogate validation when traditional methods are infeasible due to RCT scarcity.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). title: Crizotinib versus observation or placebo for surgically resected early-stage ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group-American College of Radiology Imaging Network E4512): a phase 3 trial.
abstract: Crizotinib is an established first-generation anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) inhibitor approved for the treatment of advanced ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). E4512 aimed to evaluate the effect of adjuvant crizotinib on disease-free survival (DFS) in patients with resected, early-stage ALK-positive NSCLC.In this randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial conducted in 1618 sites across the USA, Guam, and Puerto Rico, patients were randomly assigned 1:1 by computer-generated sequence to receive crizotinib 250 mg orally twice daily or observation (changed from initial double-blind placebo) for up 2 years. Eligible patients had resected NSCLC tumours that were 4 cm or larger in diameter or lymph node-positive, negative surgical margins, no neoadjuvant therapy, ALK positivity by local or central testing, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0-1. Adjuvant chemotherapy was allowed but not required. Stratification factors were stage, previous radiation therapy, and sex. The primary endpoint was disease-free survival (DFS) in the centrally tested ALK-positive intention-to-treat population and presented as hazard ratio with 90% and 95% CI. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02201992) and is completed. Safety was assessed in all patients whose tumours tested ALK-positive and who received the study drug.Between Aug 18, 2014, and May 10, 2024, 166 patients (of 168 planned) were enrolled (85 to crizotinib and 81 to observation). Accrual was stopped when the US Food and Drug Administration approved adjuvant alectinib for resected ALK-positive NSCLC. Overall, 153 (92%) patients had centrally confirmed ALK-positive tumours. Among these 153 individuals, 99 (65%) were female, 54 (35%) were male, and 121 (79%) were White. After a median follow-up of 65·7 months (IQR 37·5-85·6), median DFS was 74·6 (95% CI 71·2 to not assessable) months in the crizotinib group and 75·1 (64·7 to NA) months in the observation group (HR 1·08 [90% CI 0·67-1·73; 95% CI 0·61-1·90; p=0·80). In the crizotinib group, 46 (58%) patients had grade 3 or higher adverse events of any attribution (most commonly diarrhoea, in eight [10%] patients; oedema, in four [5%] patients; and hypertension, in four [5%] patients), including one death that was not deemed treatment-related. 21 (27%) patients had serious adverse events, most commonly dyspnoea (three [4%] patients), abdominal pain (two [3%] patients), thromboembolic event (two [3%] patients), diarrhoea (two [3%] patients), dehydration (two [3%] patients), and hypertension (two [3%] patients).Adjuvant crizotinib does not prolong DFS in patients with surgically resected ALK-positive NSCLC. title: Chromosome 1q Gain Defines a Plasma Cell-Dominant Adverse-Risk Subtype in AL Amyloidosis With Inferior Long-Term Survival.
abstract: The prognostic relevance of multiple myeloma (MM)-defined high-risk (HR) cytogenetic abnormalities in AL amyloidosis is incompletely defined. We retrospectively evaluated 517 newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis patients seen at Mayo Clinic between 2012 and 2021 who had baseline plasma cell FISH. HR cytogenetics were defined as t(4;14), t(14;16), t(14;20), del(17p), or 1q gain/amplification (+1q). HR abnormalities were identified in 151 patients (29%); +1q accounted for most HR cases (122/151, 81%). Compared with standard-risk (SR), patients harboring +1q demonstrated a greater clonal disease burden, including higher dFLC and bone marrow plasma cells, greater intact immunoglobulin secretion, higher plasma cell proliferative index, and enrichment for modified SLiM-CRAB features. Hematologic and organ response patterns of +1q patients were generally comparable to SR patients, whereas non-1q HR patients had a higher proportion of early hematologic responses. Patients harboring +1q demonstrated significantly inferior overall survival (OS) compared with both non-1q HR patients and SR patients (median OS 57 months vs. not reached vs. 120 months, p = 0.02). In multivariable piecewise Cox analysis, the adverse prognostic impact of +1q was most evident beyond 24 months from diagnosis (HR 2.89, 95% CI 1.64-5.09, p < 0.001), whereas non-1q HR lesions were not independently prognostic. These findings suggest that +1q identifies a biologically distinct AL amyloidosis subset characterized by plasma cell-dominant features and inferior long-term disease control. In contrast, other MM-defined HR cytogenetic abnormalities appear to have limited prognostic relevance in AL amyloidosis.© 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

title: Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support in High-Risk Cardiac Surgery: Contemporary Practice and Insights From U.S. Transplant Centers.
abstract: To date, evidence regarding the role of temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) for high-risk cardiac surgery (HRCS) is limited and continues to evolve. We aimed to appraise current evidence and characterize contemporary use of tMCS in HRCS across selected U.S. Transplant Centers.The authors have conducted a cross-sectional survey for tMCS use for HRCS. This survey was conducted using the RedCap system evaluating the timing of support, device selection, and technical considerations. The response rate was 74%.For isolated coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) patients with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 25%-35%, no-tMCS and intra-aortic balloon pump were the common approaches. In isolated CABG patients with LVEF less than 25%, more surgeons consider tMCS use including Impella 5.5. For CABG with mitral repair or replacement, more surgeons consider the use of tMCS. The annual volume of Impella 5.5 use for HRCS cases was ≤ 10 cases annually. For arterial access for Impella 5.5, the rate of trans-aortic and trans-axillary approach were equal. For HRCS, the simultaneous approach was more predominant, and most surgeons advance Impella to the left ventricle after the cross-clamp is off. Most surgeons leave Impella 5.5 for 72 h to 1 week. For patients with severe aortic insufficiency, one-fourth of surgeons have performed Impella 5.5 insertion.Contemporary practice demonstrates increasing adoption of tMCS use in HRCS with a trend toward preemptive implementation of support. Given limited high-quality evidence and variability in practice, careful patient selection, technical expertise, and institutional experience remain critical to achieving optimal results.© 2026 International Center for Artificial Organ and Transplantation (ICAOT) and Wiley Periodicals LLC.

title: Daratumumab, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed multiple myeloma: MAIA final survival analysis.
abstract: In previous analyses of MAIA, daratumumab plus lenalidomide/dexamethasone (D-Rd) significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival (OS) versus lenalidomide/dexamethasone (Rd) in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM). We report results on long-term OS and subsequent antimyeloma therapies from the MAIA final analysis. A protocol amendment (July 20, 2021) led to a long-term extension of MAIA, during which patients were followed for OS. A total of 737 patients were randomized to D-Rd (n = 368) or Rd (n = 369). At a median follow-up of 89.3 months (range, 0.0-102.2; interquartile range, 85.3-93.0), median OS was 90.3 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 80.8-not estimable [NE]) with D-Rd versus 64.1 months (56.0-70.8) with Rd (hazard ratio [HR], 0.67; 95% CI, 0.55-0.82); estimated 7-year OS rates were 53.1% (95% CI, 47.8-58.2) and 39.3% (34.1-44.5), respectively. Median time to subsequent antimyeloma treatment was not reached (95% CI, 84.1-NE) for D-Rd versus 42.4 months (33.5-50.6) for Rd (HR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.41-0.63; P < 0.0001). Death due to adverse events occurred in 84 patients (D-Rd, n = 44/364 [12%]; Rd, n = 40/365 [11%]). With >7 years of follow-up, D-Rd demonstrated a new benchmark for median OS (7.5 years) in transplant-ineligible NDMM, further supporting frontline D-Rd use to maximize survival.© 2026. llm_summary: The MAIA trial tested whether adding daratumumab (a cancer-fighting antibody) to a standard two-drug treatment improved survival in transplant-ineligible patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma. Patients receiving the three-drug combination lived a median of 7.5 years compared to 5.3 years with the standard treatment alone. These results suggest that the three-drug approach offers a meaningful survival benefit for this patient population.
llm_summary_expert: The MAIA trial randomized 737 transplant-ineligible patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma to receive daratumumab plus lenalidomide/dexamethasone (D-Rd) or lenalidomide/dexamethasone alone (Rd), with primary endpoints of progression-free survival and overall survival. At a median follow-up of 89.3 months, median overall survival was 90.3 months with D-Rd compared to 64.1 months with Rd (hazard ratio 0.67), corresponding to 7-year overall survival rates of 53.1% and 39.3%, respectively. Patients receiving D-Rd also demonstrated delayed time to subsequent antimyeloma therapy, with a median not reached versus 42.4 months in the Rd group (hazard ratio 0.51). Adverse event-related deaths occurred in 12% of D-Rd patients and 11% of Rd patients, indicating comparable safety profiles between treatment arms. These results from the final long-term analysis establish daratumumab combined with lenalidomide and dexamethas.

title: Older Age, STAG2, and DNMT3A Mutations Predict Superior Posttransplant Survival in Newly Diagnosed Acute Myeloid Leukemia Treated With Venetoclax Plus Hypomethylating Agents.
abstract: Venetoclax (Ven) plus hypomethylating agents (HMA) is standard frontline therapy for newly diagnosed AML (ND-AML) patients unfit for intensive chemotherapy and is also considered in younger, fit patients. However, consolidation with allogeneic stem cell transplant (ASCT) is often required to secure durable remission. The current study examines posttransplant outcomes in patients with ND-AML treated with frontline Ven-HMA who subsequently underwent ASCT. A total of 111 ND-AML patients (58% male, 60% secondary/therapy-related, median age 70 years [range, 37-80]) received a median of 3 cycles of Ven-HMA. Mutations at the time of diagnosis included RUNX1 (18%), SRSF2 (17%), TP53 (16%), ASXL1, IDH2, K/NRAS, TET2 (14% each), STAG2 (11%), DNMT3A (8%). All patients were in CR/CRi at the time of transplant including 88% after Ven-HMA. Measurable residual disease (MRD) by flow cytometry was detectable in 18/76 (24%) patients. Donors were mostly HLA-matched unrelated (75%); 51% receiving fludarabine/melphalan conditioning and 67% posttransplant cyclophosphamide. At a median follow-up of 15 months, 42 (38%) of patients have died and 18 (16%) experienced posttransplant relapse. Median posttransplant survival was not reached (NR), with 1-, 2-, 3-year survival rates of 69%/60%/57%, respectively. On multivariate analysis, age ≥ 65 years, STAG2 mutation (STAG2 MUT ), and DNMT3A MUT were associated with superior posttransplant survival. Patients were stratified into low- (0-1 point), intermediate- (2 points), and high-risk (3 points); age < 65 years, STAG2 wild type, and DNMT3A wild type, with 3-year survival rates of 89%, 59%, and 19%, respectively (p < 0.01). Taken together, age, STAG2 MUT and DNMT3A MUT stratified posttransplant survival in Ven-HMA treated patients with ND-AML.© 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

llm_summary: Researchers examined how well patients with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia (a blood cancer) survived after receiving a drug combination called venetoclax plus hypomethylating agents followed by a stem cell transplant. Patients who were older than 65 years or carried specific genetic mutations in STAG2 or DNMT3A genes had better survival rates, with three-year survival ranging from 19% to 89% depending on risk category. title: The daily dose: Early usability of an LLM tool for patient summaries and trial matching in radiation oncology.
abstract: Radiation oncology workflows generate large volumes of electronic health record (EHR) data requiring daily synthesis. Large language model (LLM)-based automation is promising, but workflow-embedded implementations at scale remain limited. We describe the design and early usability and adoption evaluation of The Daily Dose (TDD), an LLM-driven system for automated clinical summarization and trial identification in radiation oncology.TDD delivers physician-specific email summaries each morning across three Mayo Clinic campuses using RadOnc-GPT (GPT-4o) to generate EHR-derived patient summaries and identify potentially eligible clinical trials for new or consult visits. One month post-deployment, an anonymous cross-sectional survey adapted from the System Usability Scale and Technology Acceptance Model was administered to all recipients.Fifty-five of 110 users responded (50%); 94.5% were in radiation oncology and 69.1% were attending physicians. Overall, 83.6% used TDD at least several times per week. Mean domain scores (5-point Likert) were 3.89 ± 1.04 for usability and satisfaction, 3.43 ± 1.24 for perceived usefulness, and 3.80 ± 1.17 for impact and future use. Satisfaction was significantly associated with perceived time savings (p < 0.001); 27% estimated saving ≥10 min daily. Internal consistency was high (α = 0.97). Free-text responses highlighted improved preparedness and patient-context awareness but noted occasional inaccuracies and imperfect trial matching.In this early usability and adoption evaluation, a workflow-integrated LLM summarization tool was widely adopted and generally favorably perceived. These findings reflect user perceptions; objective validation of summary accuracy, trial-matching performance, and workflow efficiency is needed to establish clinical impact.© 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V. on behalf of European Society for Radiotherapy and Oncology.

title: Doppler High-Frequency Ultrasound in Vascular Complications.
abstract: The increase in the number of injectable filler procedures has led to a rise in associated complications, with vascular compromise being the most feared. As a result, blood flow can be interrupted, leading to ischemia, necrosis or ulcerations, pulmonary embolism, blindness, and cerebral vascular injuries. In this context, Doppler high-frequency ultrasound (DHFUS) is a radiological tool that can be used to avoid, to diagnose, and to treat vascular complications. This study aims to review facial vessels anatomy and major variations, describe the examination technique, probe positions and teach how to recognize vascular occlusions, in order to avoid negative outcomes.© 2026 American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine.

llm_summary: Researchers reviewed how high-frequency ultrasound with Doppler technology, which shows blood flow, can help prevent and treat vascular complications from injectable facial filler procedures. The study describes facial blood vessel anatomy, examination techniques, and how to recognize when blood vessels become blocked, which can cause serious injuries like tissue death or blindness. This ultrasound approach offers a way to avoid, diagnose, and manage these dangerous complications from cosmetic procedures.
llm_summary_expert: The study reviews the use of Doppler high-frequency ultrasound (DHFUS) as a radiological tool for managing vascular complications associated with injectable filler procedures. DHFUS can be applied across three clinical contexts: prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of vascular compromise resulting from filler injection. The examination technique involves specific probe positions and anatomical knowledge of facial vessels to identify vascular occlusions and their variations. Vascular complications from filler procedures can result in serious sequelae including ischemia, necrosis, ulcerations, pulmonary embolism, blindness, and cerebral vascular injuries. The study aims to provide guidance on facial vessel anatomy, examination methodology, and recognition of vascular occlusions to improve clinical outcomes and avoid adverse events.

title: Words matter when talking about pain: A scoping review of humanistic approaches to SDM in cancer-related pain care.
abstract: To synthesize evidence on humanistic approach to SDM in cancer-related pain care and examine how communication shapes pain recognition, meaning, and management.We conducted a scoping review following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines searching six databases and additional sources from inception to January 2026. We used an integrated mixed-methods synthesis, combining inductive thematic analysis with a deductive classification of humanistic communication characteristics informed by established frameworks.We included 27 studies, predominantly qualitative. Humanistic approaches to SDM most frequently emphasized a supportive orientation, compassion, and attention to individual perspectives. We identified five themes presenting pain as a negotiated, relational, and communicative phenomenon rather than a purely biomedical symptom: (1) pain as a site of contestation and negotiation; (2) pain education as a missing element of care; (3) pain treatment as influenced by biases; (4) pain as emotionally unseen; and (5) pain as best supported through empathetic and collaborative care.Cancer pain communication is a relational and moral process that shapes whether and how pain is recognized, legitimized, and effectively managed. While the literature emphasizes compassionate and patient-centered practices, less attention is given to reflexive and structural dimensions influencing communication.We propose a mnemonic (WORDS) to support clinically competent cancer pain communication and provide actionable clinical guidance for validation, open dialogue, relational presence, tailored education, and shared decision-making. Integrating these practices into clinician training, patient education, and intervention designs may enhance engagement among people living with pain, reduce stigma, and improve pain outcomes.Copyright © 2026 The Authors.
